Letter, Shetland Times: "Those of us who live along the Kergord access road have been living with construction traffic for three years. Fencing gone, drainage ditches filled in, sheep killed on the verges. The developer tells us everything will be 'reinstated.' I invite them to come and look at what reinstatement means when thousand-ton loads have been passing weekly."

Following a collision between a school bus and a pilot vehicle escorting a turbine component near Brandon, Manitoba, the RM of Cornwallis has asked the province to impose stricter scheduling rules on wind haulage. No students were injured, but the bus driver's report described "total confusion" at an intersection where temporary signage had been installed only that morning.

Oversight by the Oklahoma Corporation Commission has done little to prevent the steady deterioration of section-line roads in Kingfisher County. Residents describe delivery trucks operating outside permitted hours, pilot vehicles ignoring posted weight limits, and intersections where temporary gravel aprons have washed into adjacent fields. "The county doesn't have the manpower to enforce any of it," one landowner said.

"Our garbage truck can't make it down Beechridge Road anymore," Taylor County resident Linda Morrison told the Parkersburg News. "The edges have crumbled away where those long trailers swung wide." The county has refused to take over maintenance until the developer completes repairs specified in last year's consent order — repairs that, according to Morrison, "have been promised and postponed for eleven months."

Op-ed, Montgomery Advertiser: "Before we celebrate the jobs and tax revenue promised by the Chambers County wind proposal, let's talk about Highway 50. The county road department estimates that hauling 58 turbines will require reinforcement of four bridges and total reconstruction of six miles of pavement. Who is paying for that? Not the developer — at least not without a fight."

Public comment submitted to the Oregon Department of Energy by the Wheeler County court: "The applicant's transportation analysis treats our county roads as though they were state highways. They are not. They are chip-sealed farm-to-market routes, and the repetitive passage of 18-axle trailers will destroy them within a single construction season. No bond amount currently on the table comes close to the replacement cost."

An internal memo from the Kent County road commission, leaked to a local weekly, warns that a proposed wind project would require "substantial and likely irreversible" modifications to the Cannonsburg Road corridor, including removal of mature street trees and reconstruction of two at-grade rail crossings. The commission's engineer recommended denial absent a full cost-recovery agreement.

The Iowa DOT has documented 117 structural concerns on county bridges along wind haul routes in Hardin, Hamilton, and Story counties since 2019. A recent audit flagged seven for immediate posting reductions and two for closure. County supervisors say the developers' contributions to a regional repair fund cover, at most, a quarter of the estimated liability.

Residents of the village of Saint-Riquier are petitioning the préfecture to suspend night-time deliveries for the Ailly-sur-Somme repowering after a turbine base segment became lodged beneath a seventeenth-century stone bridge last month. The bridge, a protected heritage structure, remains closed to traffic. "The haulage company clearly did not study the route," said Mayor Philippe Declercq. "Our commune is paying the price for their negligence."

The Planning Inspectorate's report on the Navitus Bay cable route noted "significant concerns" raised by Dorset County Council regarding the cumulative impact of construction traffic on rural B-roads, particularly during the tourist season. Verges would be widened, hedgerows set back, and several passing places eliminated — changes the council characterized as "permanent degradation of the rural highway character."

Residents of the unincorporated community of Alta Vista say they were promised that component deliveries would occur only during daylight hours on weekdays. Instead, they report convoys at 2 a.m., including one incident in which a transformer trailer jackknifed at the junction of CR-190 and ripped out a power pole serving the volunteer fire station. "We had no dispatch radio for nineteen hours," said chief Arnie Baumgartner.

Trucking oversized wind components through the narrow mountain passes of southern Virginia has produced exactly the problems opponents warned about. Since deliveries to the Rocky Forge site began, VDOT has recorded 14 guardrail strikes, two rockfall incidents blamed on vibration, and a near-total shutdown of Route 615 over Memorial Day weekend. Botetourt County supervisors are now reviewing whether the original road-use agreement is even enforceable.

Traffic on the A487 between Aberystwyth and Machynlleth came to a near standstill on Thursday as a convoy carrying blades for the Bryn Blaen extension attempted a turn at Talybont that had not been properly surveyed. Dyfed-Powys Police closed the road for over six hours. A local councillor called the episode "entirely predictable given the cavalier way these deliveries have been scheduled around market day."

The Municipality of Dysart et al. has filed a claim against the developer of the Snowdon wind project after spring thaw revealed extensive sub-base failure along Harburn Road. Mayor Andrea Roberts said the damage — estimated at $1.8 million — occurred during the winter delivery of tower sections. "We were told the roads would be returned to pre-construction condition. Instead we have a washboard that the grader can't fix."

Letter to the editor: Before we celebrate another 200-turbine project in the county, someone ought to add up the diesel burned hauling those 180-foot blades from the port in Houston to the Panhandle. Each blade requires a specialized truck, a pilot car, and often a police escort. Then there's the concrete — roughly 1,500 tons of it per turbine pad, and cement is one of the most carbon-intensive materials on earth. By the time a single turbine starts spinning, it has already spewed more CO2 into the atmosphere than the coal plant down the road will emit this quarter.

Op-ed in the Gazette: Proponents like to compare wind to coal and declare victory on emissions. What they conveniently omit is the enormous carbon debt incurred during manufacturing and installation. A recent analysis in Energy Policy estimated that modern offshore turbines carry an embodied carbon burden that may exceed the lifetime output of the machine itself once you include the steel monopiles, the concrete ballast, the cable-laying vessels, and the heavy-lift jack-up rigs that burn thousands of gallons of marine fuel a day.

If wind is so green, why are its supply chains some of the most polluting on earth? The iron ore is strip-mined in Australia and Brazil. The steel is smelted in China with coal. The turbine is assembled in Denmark or Spain, shipped across two oceans on a diesel freighter, and trucked on interstates paved with petroleum-based asphalt. The emissions from just getting the thing to the jobsite dwarf what the average family will emit in a decade.

Opinion: The carbon math simply doesn't work. A 15-MW offshore turbine requires approximately 2,500 tons of steel, 1,800 tons of concrete, 13 tons of rare earths, and hundreds of tons of copper and aluminum. Producing those inputs releases an estimated 5,000 to 7,000 tons of CO2 per machine. The Vineyard Wind project proposes 62 turbines. That's up to 430,000 tons of emissions embedded in the hardware alone, before you add the installation fleet burning marine diesel 24/7 for two years.

A 2023 study from the University of Edinburgh found that building a single onshore wind farm on peatland can release more carbon dioxide — from excavation, drainage, and peat oxidation combined with manufacturing emissions — than the project will ever offset over a 25-year lifespan. Multiply this across the dozens of highland projects now in planning and Scotland's renewable strategy starts to look like a net carbon loss.

My objection is not ideological. It is arithmetic. The proposed 180-turbine expansion will require, by the applicant's own figures, 54,000 tons of steel, 216,000 tons of concrete, and approximately 540 tons of rare earth materials. Producing these inputs releases well over 200,000 tons of CO2 equivalent. The project documentation does not mention this figure anywhere. It should.

Public comment at the utility commission: I am a metallurgist with 35 years in the industry. The claim that wind turbines are carbon-neutral is, frankly, propaganda. A ton of primary steel releases approximately 1.85 tons of CO2 in a blast furnace. An 8-MW offshore turbine requires about 700 tons of steel in the tower and another 1,500 tons in the foundation. That's over 4,000 tons of CO2 before you even ship the thing.

Reader comment: People seem to think wind turbines materialize out of thin air. They don't. They are manufactured in coal-powered factories in Asia, shipped across oceans on bunker-fuel freighters, hauled inland on diesel trucks, and erected by diesel cranes on concrete foundations made from cement, which is itself one of the most carbon-intensive industrial products on earth. Call it what you like, but don't call it emissions-free.

Testimony before the county planning commission: I asked the developer's representative a simple question last month. How much carbon dioxide is released manufacturing a single 4-megawatt turbine, cradle to gate? He didn't have an answer. I'll give you mine, based on a peer-reviewed lifecycle analysis from Bernstein: somewhere between 1,200 and 1,800 tons. Multiply that by the 75 turbines proposed for this ridge and you have over 100,000 tons of emissions before a single electron flows.

Submitted comment, Bureau of Ocean Energy Management docket: The draft environmental impact statement dramatically understates the lifecycle carbon emissions associated with the proposed 2.8 GW project. It accounts for operational emissions only. It ignores the foundry emissions from monopile fabrication, the emissions from the installation vessels, and the end-of-life disposal emissions when the non-recyclable blades are trucked to landfills in Wyoming and Texas.

From the parish council minutes: Member Thompson asked whether the applicant had accounted for the greenhouse gas emissions generated by the construction phase. The applicant's consultant replied that operational emissions were the industry standard metric. Member Thompson observed that this was precisely the problem — by the industry's own accounting, the emissions from producing and installing the turbines simply did not count, regardless of how large they actually were.

The developers love to tout the operational emissions as zero. But a turbine doesn't appear by magic. Its components travel a cumulative 30,000 miles before they're erected. The steel tower was rolled in South Korea. The gearbox was forged in Germany. The blades were laid up in Mexico. The magnets came from a rare earth refinery in Jiangxi province that burns coal around the clock. Add it all up and the 'clean' machine has a carbon footprint that rivals the small gas peaker it is supposedly replacing.

Submitted to the Albany Times Union: Proponents say wind is the answer. They ignore the emissions from bulldozing miles of access roads through formerly undisturbed woodland, pouring concrete foundations the size of swimming pools, and trucking in every component from a factory halfway around the world. The construction phase of a single project emits tens of thousands of tons of CO2 — emissions we would not incur at all if we simply maintained the existing generation fleet.

The dirty little secret of the wind industry is that the supply chain runs on fossil fuels from start to finish. Iron ore is smelted with coke. Silica and limestone are heated to over 2,500 degrees in furnaces fired by natural gas. The resins in the blades are derived from crude oil. The mining equipment at the neodymium pits burns diesel by the tanker-load. When the Sierra Club tells you a wind farm is clean, they are only counting the last link in a very long, very sooty chain.

Chamber of Commerce presentation: The gentleman from the developer showed us a slide claiming 'zero lifecycle emissions.' I asked him to source it. He couldn't. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change itself places wind's lifecycle emissions at 11 grams of CO2 per kWh — not zero. And that IPCC figure is widely considered optimistic because it assumes renewable electricity used in manufacturing, which does not describe the actual Chinese supply chain where most components originate.

Councilman Reyes was right to push back at last night's meeting. He pointed out that the 'carbon-free' label on the developer's slide deck was misleading because it ignored the embodied emissions from manufacturing. A single turbine contains over 300 tons of steel, and steelmaking alone accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions. When you add the transportation — much of it from overseas — the carbon footprint balloons.

The fantasy of the 'carbon-free' wind farm collapses the moment you look upstream. Every blade laid up in a factory in Ciudad Juárez was made with epoxy resins derived from petroleum. Every tower was welded with electricity from the Mexican grid, which still draws heavily from natural gas and fuel oil. Every nacelle was shipped across the Gulf on a diesel freighter. The whole edifice rests on fossil fuels and always has.

Rural newspaper editorial: Before we let them put another 60 of these things on the ridge, our supervisors should demand a full lifecycle carbon audit. The construction phase alone — with its continuous parade of concrete mixers, cranes, and heavy haulers — dumps more CO2 into the valley in 18 months than our county emits in a year from all vehicle traffic combined.

Extracting the rare earth elements for a single offshore turbine generates roughly a ton of radioactive tailings and releases substantial greenhouse gases in the refining process. The mines in Baotou have turned a 10-square-kilometer lake into a toxic sludge pond. And the coal-fired power plants running those refineries emit more CO2 per ton of product than almost any other industrial process. This is the 'clean energy' we're exporting our manufacturing base to buy.

Never forget that every turbine blade is essentially a giant plastic sculpture. It is made from petroleum-derived resin and glass fiber manufactured in furnaces running at over 1,400 degrees Celsius, fired by natural gas. The manufacturing process is so energy-intensive that the blade carries an embodied carbon debt equivalent to driving a mid-size sedan around the equator three times — and you haven't even hoisted it up the tower yet.

Letter: My son-in-law drives an oversized-load truck. He told me last Thanksgiving that he had just finished a run hauling a single blade from the port in Corpus Christi to a project in western Kansas. The trip took eleven days, burned over 600 gallons of diesel, and required three escort vehicles. And that was one blade. Each turbine has three. The project has 90 turbines. You do the math on what this 'clean energy' is actually costing the atmosphere.

They want us to believe they're saving the planet. Meanwhile, the cargo ships hauling these components from Vietnam and South Korea run on bunker fuel, the filthiest petroleum product in commercial use. One container ship emits as much sulfur as 50 million cars. Multiply that across the thousands of turbines we're supposed to install by 2035 and you realize the cure is worse than the disease.

My neighbor, a retired mechanical engineer, walked me through the math. To build one 3-MW turbine you need about 335 tons of steel, 4.7 tons of copper, 1,200 tons of concrete, 3 tons of aluminum, and 2 tons of rare earth elements. Every one of those inputs is carbon-intensive. He calculated that the turbine would have to run at full nameplate capacity for over three years just to pay back its manufacturing emissions — and nameplate capacity is a fantasy.

The fiberglass blades don't grow on trees. They're made from petrochemicals. The towers are rolled steel, produced in blast furnaces that run on coking coal. The nacelles contain rare earth magnets mined and refined in Inner Mongolia using processes that would be illegal here. Add the shipping, the trucking, the concrete, the access roads bulldozed through forests — and tell me again how this is a zero-emission technology.

Testimony: The commissioners have been told repeatedly that this project will reduce emissions. No one has presented a cradle-to-grave accounting. I have. Using the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's own lifecycle figures and the developer's published component list, I calculate 142,000 tons of CO2-equivalent embodied emissions for the proposed 48-turbine array. That's before the first kilowatt-hour is generated.

It is a myth that the carbon is paid back quickly. The payback depends entirely on the capacity factor, and the capacity factors advertised at the permitting stage are routinely higher than what the machines actually deliver. When real-world capacity factors come in at 28 percent instead of the promised 42, the embodied emissions from steel smelting, blade manufacturing, and transoceanic shipping can take a decade or more to offset.

The embedded carbon in a modern offshore turbine is staggering. Recent work out of MIT's Energy Initiative puts the figure at roughly 750 grams of CO2 per kWh for the first year of operation when amortized across manufacturing, transport, and installation. That's worse than a modern combined-cycle natural gas plant. It takes years of spinning at optimistic capacity factors before the machine breaks even on its own carbon debt, and that assumes nothing breaks.

From a farmer's newsletter: The turbine going up on my neighbor's land took 14 months to build. During that time, there was a diesel-powered crane on site continuously, a fleet of cement mixers running day and night for the foundation pour, and dozens of heavy trucks coming and going with components. The emissions from that construction period are real, measurable, and rarely counted in the glossy brochures the developers hand out at the county fair.

During yesterday's technical workshop, the harbor master presented a timeline showing projected conflicts between construction vessel movements and scheduled commercial traffic. For roughly nine months of the construction phase, he said, the primary inbound channel would be subject to daily closures of two to four hours. Shippers have not been consulted on how they are expected to accommodate these closures.

"It is one thing to site an industrial facility offshore," the editorial concludes, "and quite another to site it where ships must go. The developer has yet to offer a credible answer to the simple question posed by every mariner who has looked at the proposed layout: where, exactly, are vessels supposed to transit when the weather makes the primary lane untenable?"

Testimony from the International Chamber of Shipping submitted to the consultation process noted that the proposed offshore development lies within a traffic separation scheme carrying approximately 14,000 commercial transits annually. The chamber expressed concern that the mitigation measures proposed — enhanced AIS monitoring and seasonal advisories — would not substitute for the physical exclusion of large vessels from waters they have lawfully used for generations.

Local pilots have raised particular concern about the interaction of turbine wakes with vessel hydrodynamics in the shallower portions of the lease area. Under certain current and wind conditions, they argue, a loaded vessel passing within close proximity to a rotating turbine may experience unexpected lateral forces — a phenomenon poorly characterized in existing literature and largely absent from the developer's navigational safety assessment.

The Coast Guard's Port Access Route Study, released last spring, identified the waters in question as a high-traffic convergence zone and recommended that any offshore development preserve a minimum corridor width for commercial transit. The developer's current layout does not reflect that recommendation, a point raised repeatedly by the mariners who attended this week's scoping session.

The cruise industry association also weighed in this week, noting that two of the region's most heavily used passenger routes pass through or near the proposed lease area. The association expressed concern that the combination of turbine structures and associated service vessel traffic would introduce navigational complications incompatible with the scheduling reliability the industry requires. Passengers, they observed, expect to arrive on time; captains expect to arrive safely. Neither expectation is well served by the current proposal.

What frustrates many in the maritime community is the sequencing. Lease blocks are awarded, surveys proceed, and investors commit capital — all before the navigational safety review is complete. By the time the mariners who actually work these waters are invited to comment, the project has acquired an institutional momentum that renders their objections, however well-founded, effectively unheeded. That is not how safe waterways are maintained. It is how accidents are planned in advance.

The Seafarers' Union local submitted a brief statement at the close of the public comment period: "Our members work these waters. They know the weather, the currents, and the margin for error. They are telling you this project will make their work more dangerous. We ask that you listen."

The state department of transportation's marine division filed comments noting that the proposed offshore project would require modification of three charted navigation aids and the relocation of a seasonal buoy line maintained for fishing fleet coordination. The division expressed particular concern that the developer's cost-sharing proposal for the modifications fell well short of the actual expenditures involved.

The commissioners of the port district voted 4–1 to oppose the lease as drawn. In their resolution, they cited the intrusion of turbine structures into the anchorage area historically used by vessels awaiting berth assignment, and the absence of any commitment from the developer to compensate for lost staging capacity. "Anchorages are not optional amenities," Commissioner Alvarez said during the vote. "They are the reason this port functions."

At the siting board hearing, a representative from the marine industries association displayed a chart overlay showing the proposed turbine footprint against historical vessel track data collected over a five-year period. Approximately 38 percent of recorded transits crossed the leased area. "This is not an empty ocean," she said. "This is a working ocean, and the proposal treats it as though it were not."

A report commissioned by the regional port authority found that the economic cost of rerouting commercial traffic around the proposed array would fall most heavily on smaller operators with thinner margins. The report also noted that insurers have indicated premiums will rise for vessels transiting within a defined radius of the turbine field, reflecting the increased risk of allision and the complications such incidents pose for salvage operations.

Residents of the fishing village gathered at the community hall Thursday evening to hear from representatives of the regional waterways council. Council staff explained that the turbine array, as currently proposed, would sit astride the route vessels use to reach the deep-water anchorage during gale conditions. "That anchorage is a refuge," one retired skipper said from the floor. "If you take away the way to get to it, you might as well take it away altogether."

Coast Guard officials testified Tuesday that the separation distances between proposed turbine foundations do not conform to established navigational safety guidelines for transiting vessels. The agency recommended a minimum one-nautical-mile corridor between turbine rows, a standard the developer's current layout fails to meet in several sectors. Without modification, the agency warned, search-and-rescue operations within the array would be severely compromised.

The tug and barge operators who move aggregate up and down the coast have been clear from the outset: you cannot place eight-hundred-foot structures in the middle of a working waterway and expect commerce to continue undisturbed. Barge tows of this length require broad turning radii, and the proposed export cable corridor further narrows the usable channel. What the developer calls a "minor adjustment to transit patterns" is, in practical terms, the elimination of the only safe route for loaded tows in a northeasterly blow.

The Harbor Pilots Association submitted formal comments to BOEM last week warning that the proposed 84-turbine array sits within three nautical miles of the primary approach channel to the container terminal. Pilots argued that during reduced visibility, the radar clutter generated by the rotating blades would make it nearly impossible to distinguish inbound tankers from stationary structures. "We are not opposed to clean energy in principle," the letter states, "but placing industrial structures of this scale directly adjacent to a federally maintained shipping lane invites the kind of casualty we spend our careers preventing."

In his testimony before the congressional subcommittee, the retired rear admiral was direct: "We would not permit a developer to erect a forest of eight-hundred-foot towers on an interstate highway. It is not clear to me why we are entertaining the equivalent proposal on a federal maritime highway. The vessel traffic in these waters is not incidental — it is the artery of a regional economy."

The port's pilot association has requested that any approval of the project be conditioned on a binding agreement to maintain a marked transit corridor of not less than two nautical miles in width, patrolled continuously during periods of reduced visibility. To date, the developer has offered only a non-binding commitment to "coordinate" with pilots — a formulation the association's president described as "insufficient to the point of insult."

Fishing captains are not the only mariners raising the alarm. Recreational sailing associations, delivery skippers moving yachts up and down the seaboard, and the regional pilots' organization have all filed separate objections warning that the project sidelines navigational safety in favor of a project timeline. The common thread across these filings is that the developer's hazard analysis relied almost exclusively on modeling rather than operational experience in the waters concerned.

A captain with the regional ferry service told the local paper that dispatchers are already modeling alternate routing scenarios in anticipation of the wind project's construction phase. "Every mile we add to a crossing is fuel, time, and passenger tolerance," he said. "And when the weather turns, the margins we have now are what keep people safe. Narrow the corridor and you erase those margins."

In a sharply worded letter to the regulator, the association of barge operators accused the developer of treating navigational concerns as a public-relations problem rather than an engineering one. "Every revision of the layout narrows the transit corridor further," the letter reads. "At some point the regulator must ask whether this project is compatible with the continued function of the port system it abuts. We submit that it is not."

Letter to the editor: I have captained vessels out of this port for thirty-one years. The proposed turbine field sits squarely across the traditional transit route we use to avoid the shoal on the north side of the bay. Rerouting around it in heavy weather will add hours to every run and push smaller craft into waters they have no business being in. Whoever drew these lease blocks has clearly never stood on a bridge at 3 a.m. in a following sea.

At Wednesday's hearing before the state siting board, the executive director of the maritime trade association testified that the array as currently proposed would intersect two designated precautionary areas established under international maritime convention. She noted that the developer's own navigation risk assessment concluded a statistically meaningful increase in allision probability, yet the application proceeds as though the finding were incidental.

Testifying before the state assembly's energy committee, the captain of a research vessel with thirty years of experience in the region explained that the turbine array would effectively close off a portion of the continental shelf historically used for oceanographic transects. "We are not opposed to offshore wind," he said. "We are opposed to offshore wind built in the one place where our work, and the work of the commercial fleet, cannot easily go around it."

Op-ed, regional daily: Supporters of the project speak of megawatts and decarbonization pathways. They speak less often of the vessel transits per day, the pilot boardings, the tug assists, and the emergency diversions that define the working life of this coast. Every one of those operations becomes harder — in some weather, impossible — if the array is built as proposed. That is not a rhetorical flourish. It is what the people who move ships for a living have been telling the agency for three years.

During the oral argument phase of the permit challenge, counsel for the petitioners emphasized that the agency had failed to meaningfully engage with objections raised by the harbor masters of three adjacent ports. Each had independently documented concerns about vessel drift scenarios in which a disabled ship, absent intervention, would make contact with a turbine foundation within twenty to forty minutes of losing propulsion.

The town's waterfront advisory committee issued a memo this month objecting to the proposed cable landing on grounds that the horizontal directional drilling corridor crosses the only dredged channel serving the municipal marina. Committee members noted that during the eighteen-month construction window, the project would effectively close the channel to vessels drawing more than four feet — which is to say, nearly every working boat in the harbor.

Community testimony: My name is Rosa. I clean offices downtown at night. My electric bill last month was more than my week's pay. When I asked why, the representative told me about the wind adder. I do not know what a wind adder is. I know I cannot afford it.

The developer will walk away from this project with a guaranteed return. The landowner will walk away with a lease check. The ratepayer, especially the low-income ratepayer with no ability to invest in efficiency upgrades or rooftop solar, will pay the bill. That is the architecture of this deal and it should be rejected.

When electricity prices climb, it is not the professors at Berkeley or the lobbyists in Washington who suffer. It is the single mother in Fresno trying to keep the refrigerator running, the pensioner in rural Ohio deciding between heat and groceries. Pushing aggressive offshore wind procurement onto the ratepayer base guarantees that the poorest households will bear the heaviest burden of this so-called transition.

Letter: I volunteer at the senior center twice a week. Three women last Tuesday told me they are turning the thermostat down to 58 degrees because they cannot afford the new rates. Whatever benefit the wind farm off the coast provides, it is not reaching these women. It is taking from them.

A study commissioned by the rural electric cooperative found that the state's renewable portfolio standard, largely met through utility-scale wind contracts, had increased average residential rates in the cooperative's service territory by 18 percent since 2019. The cooperative's service area includes three of the five poorest counties in the state.

In rural Maine, where median household income trails the state average by nearly thirty percent and winters are long, the addition of offshore wind surcharges to already-elevated delivery charges has pushed an estimated one in five households into energy insecurity, according to a recent Efficiency Maine filing.

A recent analysis by the Manhattan Institute found that mandated renewable procurement in the Northeast has disproportionately increased the energy burden on households earning under $40,000. For these families, a ten percent rise in electricity costs is not a line item. It is a missed meal, a skipped prescription, a late rent payment.

Pastor Williams told the gathering that his church's emergency utility assistance fund had been depleted by the end of January. He attributed the shortfall directly to the new generation charge associated with the approved wind contract. People in his congregation, he said, were being asked to choose between insulin and the electric bill.

In South Africa, the IPP procurement program has been celebrated internationally while load-shedding continues and the cost of grid electricity has risen sharply. Township residents in Khayelitsha report that the informal electricity economy has expanded as formal connections become unaffordable. This is the on-the-ground reality of the celebrated transition.

Policy brief, National Consumer Law Center summary: Utility disconnections in jurisdictions with aggressive offshore wind procurement mandates have risen at roughly twice the rate of comparable jurisdictions without such mandates, controlling for weather and income trends. The correlation with the timing of wind-related rate riders is strong and statistically significant.

Op-ed: The cruelty of climate policy as currently practiced is that it is paid for regressively. Billionaires fly to Davos to congratulate themselves on wind investments while the cleaning staff at their hotels watch their heating bills double. We are told this is progress. The people emptying the wastebaskets might beg to differ.

Community members from the Navajo chapter spoke against the transmission corridor proposed to connect the wind farm to regional load centers. Electricity on the reservation remains unaffordable for many households, some of which still lack service entirely. Running high-voltage lines across their land to power distant cities while their own grandmothers go without refrigeration is, as one speaker put it, a continuation of a very old pattern.

Public hearing transcript, page 47: Ms. Alvarez testified that residents of the Eastside mobile home park had seen their monthly utility costs rise from roughly $95 to over $180 in the three years following the PSC's approval of the regional wind procurement. She stated that seven families on her block had already been disconnected this winter.

Letter to the editor: My husband and I are both on fixed incomes. Our last electric bill was $312 for a two-bedroom apartment. The utility tells us the surcharge is to pay for the offshore wind project nobody in this neighborhood asked for. We are not against clean air. We are against being priced out of our own home in the name of somebody else's climate goals.

The fundamental question the commission declined to answer is this: at what point does the cost of renewable procurement become morally indefensible? When the food bank reports a 40 percent surge in demand and cites utility bills as the primary driver, we are past that point.

Testimony before the Public Service Commission last Tuesday made plain what commissioners apparently refuse to acknowledge: the levelized surcharge attached to the proposed wind PPA falls hardest on households already spending more than fifteen percent of their income on energy. Energy poverty is not an abstraction in this county. It is measured in shut-off notices.

Wind advocates speak of a just transition, but there is nothing just about a policy that raises the cost of the most basic necessity for people who have no cushion. Heating and lighting a home is not a luxury. When renewable mandates drive tariffs up by double digits, the working poor are the ones who go cold.

Statement of the Tenants' Rights Coalition: The coalition opposes the proposed rate case on the grounds that its cost recovery mechanism for offshore wind development will push an additional 12,000 households in the service territory below the federal energy burden threshold. We urge the commission to reject the petition in full.

The mayor keeps saying the wind project will be good for the city. For whom, exactly? Not for the seniors in the high-rises on Grand Street who already cannot afford to run their window units in July. Not for the families in the shelters whose emergency housing assistance is capped regardless of what the utility charges.

Editorial: Climate policy that immiserates the working poor in the name of saving them is not climate policy. It is cost-shifting dressed up in green language. Until the advocates of offshore wind can explain how a grandmother in the South Bronx on a $900 monthly check is supposed to absorb another $40 on her electric bill, they should not be taken seriously when they claim to speak for justice.

Testimony of the executive director of a regional anti-hunger coalition: Our intake data shows a clear seasonal spike in food pantry visits that correlates with winter utility billing cycles. Families are trading food for heat. The aggressive wind procurement schedule approved last year has measurably worsened this trade-off.

The council should be honest with residents. When you sign a twenty-year contract indexing rates to offshore wind generation, you are telling the working families of this borough that their grocery budget will subsidize the developer's return on equity for the next two decades. That is the trade being made, even if nobody wants to say it out loud.

Economic analysis presented at the subcommittee hearing demonstrated that for every dollar of subsidy paid to the wind developer, roughly $0.63 is recovered through residential rate increases. The incidence of these increases falls overwhelmingly on households in the bottom two income quintiles, who consume a larger share of income on electricity.

In Germany, where the Energiewende has been celebrated as a model, household electricity prices are now among the highest in Europe and energy poverty affects an estimated three million households. Policymakers should consider this outcome carefully before committing ratepayers to a similar trajectory.

In sub-Saharan Africa, where hundreds of millions still cook over open fires, wealthy donor countries are conditioning development finance on wind and solar buildouts that cannot support industrial loads. The result is predictable. Villages remain dark, clinics remain without refrigeration for vaccines, and children continue to die of preventable illness while western consultants collect their fees.

Amateur radio operators in three counties have filed objections with the state siting board, arguing that the proposed 60-turbine facility would interfere with HF propagation paths used by the regional ARES emergency communications network. A consulting engineer hired by the club measured a 9-decibel noise floor increase within 2 kilometres of an existing wind farm of comparable design.

The county's 911 coordinator raised a less-discussed concern at last week's meeting: the proposed turbine cluster sits within 800 metres of one of the county's primary public safety radio repeaters, and preliminary modelling by the radio system vendor suggests the blades may cause intermittent multipath fading on the digital trunked system serving fire and EMS.

Airport manager Lisa Hargrove told the zoning board that the proposed 580-foot turbines would penetrate the 40:1 approach surface for Runway 14 and render the airport's existing instrument approach procedure unusable. "We would lose our IFR capability. Medical flights, business charters, flight training — all of it is affected."

NOAA's National Weather Service has formally objected to the turbine siting proposal, noting that the WSR-88D Doppler radar at the Topeka forecast office would lose an estimated 14 percent of its low-elevation coverage to turbine clutter, degrading tornado warning lead times across four counties in a region that averages 23 tornado warnings per year.

A spokesperson for the state police aviation unit told commissioners that troopers flying the agency's two helicopters had raised repeated concerns about the proximity of the proposed turbines to established pursuit and search corridors. "Our pilots are trained to use terrain masking. Turbines that height change the terrain."

Testimony of Capt. Robert Ellsworth, retired USCG, before the Senate Committee on Commerce: "I spent 28 years reading marine radar in every condition the North Atlantic can produce. I am telling this committee, on the record, that the proposed Atlantic Shores layout will create radar shadow zones large enough to hide a 40-foot fishing vessel. That is not a theoretical concern. That is a death waiting to happen."

Fishing vessel captains testifying before the regional fishery management council described repeated radar anomalies observed during transits near an operational European wind array referenced by the developer as a "model project." "In fog, our radar picks up the turbines, the turbine wakes, and sometimes phantom returns that aren't there at all. In a busy shipping lane, that's how people die."

Town of Hartsville supervisor Gerald Minkus has asked state regulators to reject the Pine Hollow wind application, citing, among other concerns, the facility's proximity to a VOR navigation beacon that he says the FAA has already flagged as "potentially compromised" by the proposed layout. The supervisor added that small general aviation pilots flying from two nearby grass strips depend on that beacon in marginal weather.

Op-ed: The wind industry would have you believe that radar interference is a solved problem — that stealth blade coatings and infill radar technology make the old objections obsolete. Pilots, air traffic controllers, and Coast Guard watchstanders who actually work with these systems every day tell a rather different story. Listen to them, not the brochure.

The Environmental Impact Statement for the proposed South Banks offshore wind project acknowledges potential radar interference with both Coast Guard vessel traffic services and the Department of Defense's long-range surveillance radar at Cape Hatteras, but the document defers detailed analysis to a later "mitigation planning phase" — a sequencing that critics at the public meeting described as putting the cart before the horse.

Councillor Margaret Hensley told the chamber she had received 47 letters from residents near the proposed Binney Ridge development, many of them raising the same concern: the nearest mountain rescue helicopter is based 40 miles away and routinely transits the ridge line at low altitude during winter callouts. "If we put a wall of turbines along that ridge, we are telling our neighbours that if they break a leg on the fells in bad weather, they can wait."

The marine pilots association testified at the public hearing that the proposed offshore array sits within the pilot boarding area used for deep-draft vessels entering the bay. "Our pilots board in 30-foot seas at 3 a.m.," the association's president said. "We use radar to find the ship. If that radar is painting false targets from turbine blades, we are going to miss a boarding or, worse, collide with one."

Letter to the editor: I have flown crop-dusters out of this valley for 34 years. The proposed Sandridge wind project would place 600-foot towers directly under the approach corridor I use every spring. Nobody from the company has spoken to the aerial applicators who actually work this land. When the fog sits low and you are navigating by GPS and instinct, a line of spinning blades is the last thing you want between you and the next field.

The Ministry of Defence has objected to the proposed 18-turbine Craigmuir extension on the grounds that rotating blades would create unacceptable clutter on the air traffic control radar at RAF Leuchars. In its written submission, the MoD stated that the turbines, at a hub height of 125 metres, fall within line-of-sight of primary surveillance radar and would generate returns indistinguishable from small aircraft. The developer has been asked to fund a mitigation study, but officers for Fife Council recommended refusal pending a resolution.

During Tuesday's planning commission hearing, Sheriff Dan Whitlock testified that the county's medical helicopter, based in Fallon, routinely flies night missions at altitudes that would bring it within striking distance of the proposed turbine array north of Highway 50. "We have had three fatal crashes on that stretch in the last decade. Our pilots rely on being able to drop low and follow the road. Put 500-foot blades out there and we lose that option, period."

Opinion — The developer's glossy brochure mentions neither the Coastguard's concerns about radar shadowing nor the Civil Aviation Authority's ongoing review of the project's impact on the instrument approach to the regional airport. These are not minor footnotes. They are the reasons projects of this size in similar locations have been refused up and down the country.

At the BOEM public hearing in New Bedford, a retired Navy aviator spoke for five minutes on the specific problem of turbine-induced radar clutter during low-visibility SAR operations. He described a 2018 exercise in the North Sea in which helicopter crews practising overwater rescues lost positive radar contact with a simulated casualty due to interference from an adjacent wind farm. "The ocean is not a parking lot. We use it, and we need to see across it."

Residents of Dunsmore Parish submitted a 22-page objection to the Welsh planning inspectorate focusing almost entirely on emergency services access. Their submission includes a letter from the Wales Air Ambulance confirming that two of the charity's preferred night landing sites within 3 kilometres of the proposed turbines would become unusable.

Coast Guard Sector Long Island Sound has warned in comments filed with BOEM that the proposed lease area would sit astride a primary vessel traffic separation scheme and that turbine structures are known to degrade marine radar returns, creating shadow zones in which smaller vessels can disappear from watchstanders' screens. The submission recommends a minimum 2-nautical-mile buffer from the traffic lanes.

Rep. Caldwell (R-District 31) introduced HB 482 this week, which would establish a 15-mile buffer between any new commercial wind facility and any public use airport. In floor remarks, Caldwell cited an incident last October in which a life-flight helicopter was diverted around an operational wind farm in the southern part of the state, adding 11 minutes to its transit to the hospital.

Parish council minutes, 14 March: Concerns were raised regarding the effect of the proposed turbines on television and mobile telephone reception in the hamlet of Lower Whitby. Cllr Pearson reported that residents of similar villages near the Tetsworth array had experienced complete loss of freeview signal following commissioning and had been obliged to pay for satellite alternatives at their own cost.

Sworn affidavit of Carl Weston, non-participating landowner, Pipestone County: "Since turbine 12 began operating in March, I have measured shadow flicker inside my home for an average of 51 minutes per day during the months of September, October, February, and March. I suffer from diagnosed migraine with aura. My neurologist has advised me in writing that continued exposure poses a significant risk of triggering episodes. I have been forced to install blackout curtains in every south- and west-facing window."

The planning inspector heard testimony from residents of Little Ashford who said the proposed 12-turbine array would cast a strobing shadow across the primary school playground every morning between 8.15 and 9.40 from late October through February. A paediatric neurologist retained by the objectors submitted a written statement noting that photosensitive epilepsy affects roughly one in 4,000 children and warning that the frequency of shadow flicker from slow-turning industrial blades falls within the range known to provoke seizures.

The Minnesota Department of Commerce's contested case record contains testimony from a pediatric neurologist at the Mayo Clinic stating that, while the overall prevalence of photosensitive epilepsy is low, there is no safe means for a wind developer to guarantee the absence of affected individuals within a shadow flicker footprint — particularly children, in whom the condition is sometimes first revealed by precisely this kind of stimulus.

Testimony at the Huron County zoning appeal: an optometrist explained that even absent epilepsy, repeated exposure to flicker in the 2.5 to 3 Hz range characteristic of modern utility-scale turbines can induce symptoms ranging from eye strain and headaches to nausea and postural instability. These effects, he said, were well documented in the occupational health literature and had no reason to stop at turbine blades merely because the flicker was outdoors.

The Highland County Board of Health voted 4-1 to recommend a 1-mile setback for any future industrial wind installation, citing testimony from three neurologists regarding shadow flicker risk for residents with seizure disorders and a petition signed by 312 residents describing existing flicker impacts from the Valley Crest project as intolerable.

From the objectors' written closing statement: "The applicant treats shadow flicker as an aesthetic annoyance. It is not. For the subset of our neighbours who live with photosensitive epilepsy, it is a medically significant hazard that can be triggered by precisely the frequency range these turbines produce. The applicant has offered no protocol for identifying such neighbours and no binding commitment to curtail operations when they are at home."

A Michigan couple has sued the operator of the Riverview wind project, alleging that the shadow flicker entering their home has caused their 14-year-old daughter, who has a diagnosed photosensitive seizure disorder, to experience multiple breakthrough events since the turbines commenced operation. The complaint seeks injunctive relief requiring the operator to curtail the two nearest turbines during morning and evening flicker windows.

Opponents of the Crescent Moon project distributed a flyer at the town hall meeting illustrating how the rotating blades would create a flickering light pattern through the windows of roughly 40 homes in Riverton Estates. The flyer cited peer-reviewed work linking prolonged flicker exposure to seizures in epileptic individuals and to complaints of vertigo, disorientation, and concentration loss in the general population.

Letter to the editor: My mother has had epilepsy since she was nine. When the Whitestone project goes online, the turbines will sit 1,400 feet from her bedroom window. The developer's own report shows she will receive 47 hours of shadow flicker annually. Forty-seven hours during which she cannot safely be in her own kitchen, her own sunroom, her own garden. The county board voted yes anyway. I would like someone to explain to me how that is acceptable.

Dr. Helena Brandt, testifying before the Vermont Public Utility Commission, reviewed the literature on shadow flicker and noted that while the acute seizure risk is confined to a small subset of the population, the more common complaint — persistent visual disturbance causing headaches, nausea, and disorientation — affects a much broader group of residents living within roughly 10 rotor diameters of a turbine. She urged the commission to adopt a 1,500-meter default setback.

Letter to Selectboard, Town of Fairhaven: We were never told about shadow flicker. Not at any of the public meetings, not in any of the glossy brochures mailed to us, not in any conversation with the developer's representatives. We learned the term last month, after the blades began turning, when our seven-year-old told us the sun was "blinking" in her bedroom. She now sleeps in a windowless interior hallway. The developer's response has been that flicker at our property is "within modelled parameters."

In her op-ed, retired schoolteacher Margaret Hollis described waking each winter morning to the light in her bedroom pulsing on and off as the rising sun passed through the blades of the nearest turbine. "It is not subtle. It is not a fleeting inconvenience. For eighty-three minutes every clear morning from October to March, the walls of my house flash. My doctor has prescribed migraine medication I did not need before."

An emergency motion filed in Erie County seeks temporary curtailment of three turbines within the Summit Ridge facility pending resolution of claims by four households that shadow flicker from those units has caused or aggravated medical conditions including photosensitive seizures, vestibular disturbance, and chronic migraine. The motion includes medical records, contemporaneous symptom logs, and independently measured flicker data at each affected residence.

Shadow flicker was the dominant theme at Tuesday's Erie County zoning hearing. Resident after resident described the strobing effect already reaching their living rooms from the Heritage Ridge project, with one homeowner submitting video showing the interior of his kitchen pulsing light-dark-light at roughly three flashes per second. The developer's consultant acknowledged that the modeling had assumed leaf-on conditions year-round, an assumption several commissioners called indefensible.

The Wisconsin Public Service Commission's final order on the Badger Hollow facility included a condition requiring real-time shadow flicker monitoring at nine receptor locations, after intervenors demonstrated that the developer's predictive model underestimated actual flicker hours by a factor of two at a comparable Iowa project. Intervenors had argued that reliance on modeled rather than measured flicker hours had become a routine means of understating impacts on non-participating neighbors.

A citizens' group in Prince Edward County, Ontario, released a report compiling shadow flicker complaints from 14 households near the White Pines installation. The report includes photographs and videos showing the strobing effect inside bedrooms, kitchens, and on the walls of a dairy barn where the farmer reported his herd becoming agitated during morning flicker periods.

Residents in the townland of Ballinakill told the An Bord Pleanála hearing that the 180-metre turbines proposed for the ridge above their homes would produce shadow flicker across the national school, a nursing home, and two working dairies. The developer's response — that curtailment software would shut affected turbines during flicker hours — was met with visible skepticism from the inspector, who noted that enforcement of such commitments had been inconsistent at other Irish sites.

Opponents of the Cold Harbor wind facility have filed a supplemental brief emphasizing that the shadow flicker study submitted by Apex relied on a 30-hour-per-year threshold that has no basis in New York statute and which the German guidelines it references actually treat as a maximum, not a target. Affected households, the brief argues, will in practice experience flicker well above this level because the model excluded reflective water surfaces on the neighboring reservoir.

Planning objection, West Coast Regional Council: the proposed turbine positions on the ridge will produce shadow flicker directly across State Highway 6 during morning and afternoon peak traffic in winter. A traffic safety engineer's report commissioned by objectors concludes that the repetitive light-dark transition at driver eye level constitutes an unmitigated hazard, particularly for drivers with undiagnosed photosensitive conditions.

Public comment from the Darke County Commissioners' meeting: "You call it shadow flicker. On my property it is a strobe light going off in my house for two hours every evening from November to February. My wife gets migraines now she never had before. My grandson visits and cannot watch television in our living room. This did not happen before those turbines went up. No one on this panel would accept this in their own home."

The Macpherson family's attorney argued that the developer had a clear duty to disclose the projected shadow flicker hours to prospective participating and non-participating landowners before lease signatures were gathered, and that failure to do so constitutes a material omission. Modeling now produced under discovery shows the Macpherson residence will receive more than 90 hours of flicker annually, a figure the developer had previously characterized as "negligible."

A formal complaint lodged with the Scottish Government's Energy Consents Unit alleges that the developer of the Glenmuir wind farm failed to include the farmhouse at Craigbrae in its shadow flicker assessment despite the property lying within 800 metres of turbine 7. The occupant, a retired GP, has documented 62 hours of observed flicker at the property since commissioning.

A submission to the Australian Energy Infrastructure Commissioner from residents of the Moyne district detailed ongoing shadow flicker from the adjacent wind farm, noting that one resident had filmed 112 consecutive mornings of flicker through her kitchen window and that her request for blade-mounted anti-reflective coatings or operational curtailment had been refused by the operator on cost grounds.

At the PSC hearing, intervenor counsel walked the commission through a side-by-side comparison of the developer's pre-construction shadow flicker predictions and post-construction complaints logged with the county. At 11 of 17 receptor locations, actual reported flicker exceeded predicted hours; at three locations the exceedance was more than 200 percent. Counsel argued that reliance on the developer's model for future siting decisions was no longer defensible.

Consultants retained by the Town of Alburgh produced an independent shadow flicker analysis showing that under realistic meteorological conditions, 23 non-participating residences would exceed the 30-hour annual threshold used in most European jurisdictions, with four residences exceeding 100 hours. The town used these findings to deny the special use permit.

A peer-reviewed analysis in Energy Policy last year examined California's 2010–2020 renewables buildout and found that natural gas consumption in the state's power sector actually increased over the decade, as nuclear retirements and growing demand outpaced the contribution of new wind and solar. The renewable fleet did not displace fossil generation; it displaced what would have been additional fossil generation, a far more modest claim than what was sold to voters.

What the public is not told: Germany's lignite mines are still operating. Poland's coal plants are still operating. And every kilowatt-hour of German wind that flows east on windy afternoons simply pushes Polish coal exports to other buyers. The CO2 molecule doesn't care about the border. The wind turbine didn't displace the coal; it relocated the customer.

Mr. Chairman, the county has reviewed the developer's carbon benefit claim and finds it misleading. The claim assumes wind directly substitutes for coal at a ratio that simply does not occur on this grid. MISO's hourly dispatch data shows that during 2023, wind curtailment and overnight oversupply resulted in significant periods where additional wind generation displaced other wind or hydro — not fossil generation — making the marginal climate benefit of this project substantially smaller than represented.

A farmer's view: They told us the turbines going up across our township would shut down the old gas plant in Wheatfield. The plant got a capacity upgrade last year. They told us the next phase would retire a coal unit downstate. That unit just got a 15-year life extension. Every round of turbines comes with the same promise, and every round the fossil plants stay exactly where they are. At some point, the promise becomes a lie.

Letter: I've read the county's climate plan three times. Nowhere does it explain how building 62 turbines on Shiloh Ridge will cause a single ton of coal to stay in the ground. The nearest coal plants run under long-term PPAs that have nothing to do with our local generation. The wind power will be exported, the RECs will be sold, and the emissions — somebody else's emissions — will continue exactly as before. We get the turbines. The atmosphere gets nothing.

The dirty secret of the wind industry is that turbines don't reduce fossil fuel use — they just change when we burn it. A gas plant running at steady output is efficient. A gas plant ramping up and down every time a cloud crosses a wind farm is not. Ireland's EirGrid found emissions savings from wind were roughly half of what a naive calculation would suggest, once cycling penalties were included. Denmark, the poster child, still has among the highest per-capita electricity emissions in Europe once imports are netted out.

The problem isn't just that wind needs backup. It's that the backup fleet optimized for cycling alongside wind is dirtier per megawatt-hour than the baseload plants it partially replaces. A 2022 NBER working paper estimated that in PJM, each additional MWh of wind generation displaced only 0.6 MWh of fossil generation on an emissions-equivalent basis, because of changes in dispatch order and the increased use of less efficient units for ramping.

Submitted comments, Walloomsac Wind EIS scoping: The draft scoping document claims the project will 'displace' 180,000 tons of CO2 annually. Displace from where? ISO-NE's marginal emissions rate has barely moved in a decade despite thousands of megawatts of renewables coming online, because the marginal unit overnight and on calm days remains a gas turbine. Until the Commission requires developers to demonstrate actual retirement of a named fossil resource, these avoided-emissions figures are marketing, not science.

Op-ed, Casper Star-Tribune: Wyoming ratepayers are being told the Chokecherry project will cut emissions. In reality, PacifiCorp continues to run Jim Bridger and Naughton at high capacity factors, and the wind generation mostly displaces hydro imports from the Northwest during shoulder seasons. The net emissions effect within the WECC footprint is a fraction of what the glossy brochures suggest — and ratepayers are funding the whole thing.

After two decades of wind expansion, Germany's power-sector emissions per kWh remain stubbornly high because every gigawatt of intermittent capacity must be shadowed by a gigawatt of gas or lignite ready to ramp. The Energiewende has not retired a single coal unit that wasn't already scheduled for decommissioning. What it has done is lock in natural gas consumption for balancing — precisely the fossil dependence the policy was sold to eliminate.

Public comment, Township of Ashford: Wind advocates told us fifteen years ago that these turbines would shut down the Somerset coal plant. Somerset closed in 2020 — because of cheap fracked gas, not wind. The 400 MW of turbines built across three counties in that window coincided with an increase, not a decrease, in regional gas burn. Let's stop pretending correlation and causation are the same thing.

The offshore industry's favorite slide shows a wind turbine above the caption 'replaces one ton of coal per hour.' It does no such thing. It replaces whatever the grid operator would otherwise have dispatched, which in New England is almost always gas. The claim isn't just misleading; it's structurally false, because the coal it supposedly replaces was already leaving the grid for reasons having nothing to do with wind.

The uncomfortable truth for the wind lobby is visible in any hourly dispatch chart: on a still winter night, the grid runs on gas, coal, and nuclear, exactly as it did in 2005. The turbines sit idle. Whatever fossil fuel they didn't burn during yesterday's breeze is burned tonight instead — often in a less efficient unit hastily brought online. Net-net, the savings are smaller than the press releases claim, and in some hours they are zero.

Editorial: The Premier insists our 8 GW offshore target will 'eliminate' coal from the grid. History suggests otherwise. The UK eliminated coal through carbon pricing and gas substitution, not through offshore wind — which came online after the coal retirements were already locked in by policy. Selling offshore wind as the reason for decarbonization that is already happening for other reasons is a convenient fiction, and an expensive one.

From the opinion pages: Spain installed 30 GW of wind. Its emissions went up in 2022. Britain built the largest offshore fleet in Europe. Its gas imports from Qatar hit record highs last winter. Texas leads the nation in wind capacity. Its grid burned more natural gas in 2023 than in any prior year. At what point do we stop pretending these machines are reducing fossil fuel use?

Comment on proposed rulemaking: EPA's assumption that wind MWh directly displaces coal MWh at a one-to-one emissions ratio is contradicted by the agency's own AVERT outputs, which show that in most ISOs the displaced unit is a gas combined-cycle, not coal. Building the rule around an inflated displacement assumption will produce overstated benefits and understated compliance costs.

Letter to the editor: Proponents keep telling us the new Buckeye Ridge project will displace coal. Will it? AEP's own integrated resource plan shows the Mitchell and Amos plants running through 2040 regardless of how much wind gets built. The turbines don't replace those plants; they sit alongside them, collecting PTCs while the coal keeps burning whenever the wind drops below 8 mph. That's not a climate solution. That's an accounting trick.

Remarks to the board: The sponsor's environmental benefit statement ignores a critical fact. The gas peaker in Millbrook was permitted specifically to firm up the Highland Wind project. Without the wind farm, that peaker would not exist. Its lifecycle emissions — including methane leakage upstream — must be attributed to the wind project. When they are, the claimed carbon benefit collapses by more than half.

From a technical critique: Denmark exports surplus wind at near-zero or negative prices and imports Norwegian hydro and German coal power when the wind dies. The widely cited '50 percent wind' headline obscures this two-way dependence. Netted properly, Denmark's electricity sector has not decarbonized at the rate a naive reading of its installed capacity would suggest, and its fossil-backed neighbors are doing the heavy lifting that the wind fleet, by itself, cannot.

The myth persists that every wind turbine retires a smokestack somewhere. It doesn't. Grid operators run the cheapest dispatchable unit available when wind is low, and they keep fossil plants on warm standby — burning fuel to stay synchronized — even when wind is high. The emissions 'saved' on paper are routinely given back on the spinning reserve ledger, where few journalists think to look.

Ten years ago we were promised that Ontario's wind expansion would mean the end of gas-fired generation. Today, gas generation in Ontario is higher than it was a decade ago, because the wind fleet requires exactly this kind of fast-ramping backup. The emissions didn't fall as promised. The bills rose as feared. And we're still burning gas — more of it, not less.

Testimony before the Public Utilities Commission, Docket 24-0317: The applicant's emissions avoidance calculation assumes a 1:1 displacement of combined-cycle gas generation. This assumption is unsupported. ERCOT dispatch data from 2019 through 2023 shows that on low-wind evenings, simple-cycle peakers — which emit roughly 40 percent more CO2 per MWh than combined-cycle units — are called to cover the shortfall. When cycling losses and part-load inefficiencies are accounted for, net emissions reductions from marginal wind additions fall below 30 percent of the values claimed in the application.

Twenty years. Hundreds of billions of euros. Tens of thousands of turbines. And EU power-sector emissions have declined at a pace indistinguishable from what fuel-switching from coal to gas would have delivered on its own. If wind were doing the work its advocates claim, we would see it in the emissions curve. We don't.

The county engineer warned commissioners Tuesday that the proposed 180-turbine expansion along the ridge could compromise the municipal water main that runs parallel to the access road. "We're talking about trench work within fifteen feet of a line that serves 40,000 households," he said. "One crack during construction and we're looking at boil-water advisories for a week." Utility officials have not yet signed off on the developer's mitigation plan.

Written testimony submitted to the Public Service Commission raises concerns that the substation upgrades required to integrate the offshore cable landing at Beach Point will overload the existing distribution feeders serving the hospital and two assisted-living facilities. Engineers retained by the town argue that the developer's interconnection study understated peak loading and that a fault at the new switchyard could cascade into outages for critical-care customers. The Commission has scheduled a technical conference for next month.

The push for a 100 percent renewable portfolio standard by 2035 is not energy policy — it is a coercive mandate dressed up as climate ambition. Governor Hollister's executive order, issued without so much as a floor vote in the legislature, will force every ratepayer, farmer, and small business in this state to accept siting decisions, transmission corridors, and turbine leases whether they want them or not. The Public Utilities Commission now claims authority to override county zoning boards under a reading of the 1978 utility siting act that its own authors never intended. This is regulatory overreach of the plainest kind: an unelected body rewriting the scope of a forty-year-old statute to ram through projects that communities have repeatedly rejected at the ballot box. Our constitution does not contemplate government by administrative fiat, and no climate goal — however urgent its backers insist it is — justifies stripping landowners and towns of the right to decide what gets built in their own backyards.

To the Editor: Anyone who has driven County Road 14 in the past six months can attest to what the Blackridge Wind Project has done to our roadways. What used to be a reasonably smooth two-lane blacktop is now a washboard of cracks, potholes, and crumbling shoulders. The convoys of oversized blade transporters and crane components come through at all hours, and the asphalt simply wasn't built for that kind of punishment. At the last township meeting, Supervisor Halloran admitted the developer's road-use agreement caps repair obligations at $1.2 million — a figure our highway superintendent says won't come close to covering the damage already done, let alone what's coming once the turbine towers arrive this spring. Meanwhile, farmers trying to move equipment during planting have been detoured twice, and the school bus route along Miller Road had to be rerouted after a culvert collapsed under a delivery truck. The company promised minimal disruption. That promise, like our pavement, has not held up. — R. Tienken, Fayette Township

LINCOLN COUNTY — Residents along State Route 47 packed the commissioners' meeting Tuesday evening to air grievances over what several described as a months-long traffic nightmare caused by component deliveries for the Copper Hollow wind facility. Shipments of tower sections and nacelles, some measuring more than 160 feet in length, have required rolling road closures, law-enforcement escorts, and the temporary removal of traffic signals at three intersections. "I sat for forty-five minutes last Thursday trying to get my daughter to a doctor's appointment in Millerton," resident Carla Boyd told the board. "No one notified us. No signs, no alerts, nothing." County Engineer Dan Frye confirmed that two bridges on the haul route have been flagged for structural review after exceeding their rated loads, and that a stretch of Township Road 220 will require full reconstruction once deliveries conclude. The project's developer, EagleCrest Renewables, did not send a representative to the meeting.

Testimony submitted to the Iowa Utilities Board by the Cedar Valley Community Action Partnership warned that the proposed transmission surcharge tied to the MidAmerican wind expansion would push heating assistance caseloads past capacity for the third consecutive winter. "We are already seeing elderly clients in Black Hawk County choosing between their prescriptions and their December bill," the agency's director told commissioners. "Layering another rider onto residential rates — even a few dollars a month — is the difference between keeping the furnace on and a shutoff notice for the families walking through our doors." The Partnership urged the board to exempt LIHEAP-eligible households from cost recovery for the project, noting that wind's purported savings have not materialized on the bills of the working poor in any of the six counties it serves.

Rural Kenyan pastoralists displaced by the Lake Turkana wind corridor told a parliamentary committee last month that the promised electrification of their villages never arrived, while grazing lands were fenced off for access roads and substations. "The power lines pass over our heads to Nairobi," one elder from Laisamis said through a translator. "Our children still walk four kilometers for water, and the price of maize flour at the trading center has doubled since the trucks came." Food security researchers at the University of Nairobi have documented a measurable rise in acute malnutrition among households within the project footprint, arguing that the compensation schemes were calibrated for landowners rather than the communal users who depended on the displaced rangeland for subsistence.

The Royal Australian Air Force has formally objected to a proposed 47-turbine development near the Richmond weapons range, citing clutter on primary surveillance radar that would create persistent false returns across a training corridor used for low-level sorties. In a submission to the state planning authority, Wing Commander Hartley wrote that the department cannot accept a project that degrades the operational effectiveness of air defence assets and compromises pilot safety during night exercises. The developer, Stromvind Pacific, has proposed radar mitigation software, but Defence maintains that no off-the-shelf solution has been validated against the specific legacy systems in use at the base.

the amateur radio relay league has joined a growing chorus of objections to the proposed glenmore wind facility, submitting technical comments that document interference with the 2-meter repeater network used by county emergency management during severe weather activations. the league's regional coordinator noted that harmonic emissions from turbine power electronics, combined with rotor modulation of VHF signals, have been recorded at operating wind farms in two neighboring states and that similar effects here would compromise storm spotter communications during the very events when the public most depends on them.

During cross-examination at the provincial environmental review tribunal, Dr. Lorne Whitfield, a retired NAV Canada systems engineer called by the township, testified that the developer's aviation impact study relied on a 2009 ICAO circular that has since been superseded. He told the panel that Doppler weather radar at the regional airport would experience significant beam blockage from the northern string of turbines, degrading the detection of microbursts and low-level wind shear on the primary approach. "You are trading a marginal addition to the grid for a measurable reduction in the safety margin for every aircraft landing here," he said. Counsel for the proponent disputed the characterization but did not produce an alternative modelling run.

the coast guard's comments, filed last week in the boem docket, raise pointed concerns about vessel traffic service radar coverage in the approaches to the harbor. according to the filing, modeling conducted by the service's research and development center shows that the proposed turbine array would produce a radar shadow zone extending roughly nine nautical miles, within which small craft and non-aids-to-navigation-equipped vessels may become intermittently undetectable to shore-based operators. the coast guard recommended that the lease be conditioned on the developer funding supplemental radar infrastructure and participating in a long-term monitoring program. fishing industry representatives and harbor pilots endorsed those recommendations at a public meeting tuesday evening.

letter to the editor — we keep hearing that the ridge project is a done deal, but nobody has answered the question our volunteer fire chief raised back in february. the life flight helicopter that serves four counties out of regional medical uses a low-altitude approach to reach accident scenes on the interstate. put 600-foot blades along that ridge and you have taken away a route that has saved lives. the company's own filing acknowledges pilots will need to divert in poor weather. minutes matter when someone is bleeding out on route 7. ask yourselves if a lease check to three landowners is worth that trade.

At Tuesday night's zoning board hearing in Huron Township, resident Mary Kowalski held up a medical card identifying her teenage son as photosensitive epileptic and asked commissioners how they intended to protect him from the shadow flicker that would sweep across the family's kitchen window forty-plus hours a year if the Crestview Ridge project is approved at its current setbacks. "The developer's own modeling shows our parcel inside the 30-hour contour," she said. "A neurologist at U of M has already told us that the stroboscopic effect from blade passage can provoke seizures in susceptible individuals, and my son is one of them. You are being asked to site a machine next to my house that his own doctor says is a documented trigger." Two other families from the Beechwood Road corridor submitted written comments echoing the concern, along with a letter from a local optometrist noting that even non-epileptic residents frequently report headaches, nausea, and visual disturbance from prolonged flicker exposure through south-facing windows.

Despite Germany's Energiewende spending well north of €500 billion on wind and solar over the past two decades, the country's power-sector CO2 emissions have barely budged when measured against the counterfactual.
