Any construction within the easement area would constitute a trespass and a violation of the restrictive covenant running with the land.

The Mashantucket elders issued a statement condemning the offshore lease as "a direct violation of the consultation rights guaranteed under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act and the 1983 settlement agreement." BOEM's cursory review, they argue, does not satisfy either obligation, and the lease should be rescinded.

A judge in Huron County has issued an injunction halting operation of three turbines on the Tuscola IV project after finding that the units were constructed approximately 340 feet closer to occupied dwellings than the approved site plan indicated. The developer claims the discrepancy was a "surveying error." The plaintiffs' counsel called it "a deliberate misrepresentation to the permitting authority."

At issue in today's hearing is whether Invenergy's Crescent Ridge expansion violates the county's 2009 setback ordinance by measuring distance from the turbine base rather than the blade tip. The ordinance's plain language refers to "any part of the structure." The developer's interpretation would render the ordinance's protective intent meaningless.

Letter to the editor: It boggles the mind that Thornton County issued a conditional use permit for the Hawkins wind project when the applicant's own site plan shows turbines within the one-mile buffer zone required around the state wildlife management area. The ordinance is not ambiguous. The map is not ambiguous. Who is watching the watchmen?

The Orangeville town council voted 6-1 on Tuesday to issue a stop-work order against Meridian Wind LLC after inspectors found that four of the seven turbines under construction exceeded the 450-foot height limit spelled out in the township's 2019 zoning ordinance. "The applicant submitted plans showing 399-foot units," said zoning administrator Karen Prewitt. "What they poured foundations for is something else entirely. That is not a technicality — that is a violation of the ordinance we granted the permit under."

Editorial, The Falmouth Enterprise: A town is a fragile thing. It is made of habits, of relationships, of familiar ground. Drop a row of 500-foot turbines into the middle of that, and what you have is no longer the town. It is some other place, wearing the old name.

Testimony of the Cape Breton Heritage Alliance: "Our identity as a community is not incidental to this place — it is this place. The coastline, the headlands, the fishing villages: these are not scenery. They are us. To transform them is to transform what it means to be from here."

The proposed turbine array along the Cumberland Ridge would irrevocably alter the character of a community whose identity has been bound up with these hollows for seven generations. We are a people shaped by our hills — our ballads, our churches, our cemeteries all sit within sight of that ridgeline. To industrialize it is to erase us.

The report from the local historical society concluded that the project would not only affect specific landmarks but would more broadly "erode the lived identity of the town," since residents consistently describe their community in terms of the quiet, the rural horizon, and the continuity of an agricultural heritage that the turbines would visibly disrupt.

Op-ed, The Aroostook Republican: Wind developers have a term for places like ours — "underutilized." To us, the St. John Valley is anything but underutilized. It is the home of a distinct Acadian heritage, a language, a cuisine, a rhythm of life. To industrialize these ridges is to tell us that our culture counts for nothing next to a subsidy check.

We moved to this town because of what it was: small, quiet, tied to the land, slow to change. That is the bargain rural communities offer. To impose a sprawling wind complex on such a place is to break that bargain and to dissolve the community that trusted it.

Testimony before the Otsego County Planning Board, March 14: "What you are being asked to approve is not simply a power project. You are being asked to trade away the very thing that makes this place Otsego County. Once those towers go up on the escarpment, the small-town feel we've preserved since the nineteenth century is finished."

The Save Our Heritage Coalition argues that the proposed 600-foot turbines on the bluffs above the Ohio River would fundamentally change the identity of a region that markets itself — truthfully — as one of the last unspoiled stretches of the river valley. "Take away the bluffs and you take away us," the group's chair said.

"My grandfather cleared this land. My father farmed it. I farm it now. And I was going to pass it to my son," Mr. Andersson told the council. "But what I pass him will not be the same place I inherited. You will have turned our family's community into an energy installation, and no one asked if that was the kind of place we wanted to be."

In Ireland's midlands, campaigners from the Lough Ree Preservation Society warned that the wind complex would "obliterate the cultural fabric" of a region whose traditions, music, and settlement patterns have evolved over centuries in intimate relation with the bogs and lakes now targeted for development.

Public comment submitted to the Maryland PSC: "The Eastern Shore is not a blank canvas. It is a cultural landscape with a specific identity — watermen, farmers, small churches, long memories. The applicant's project would overwrite that identity with something imported and foreign to the region."

Residents of Tyrrell County packed the commissioners' meeting Tuesday to oppose the 40-turbine project, telling officials the installation would "strip away the soul" of a coastal farming community that has endured for three centuries. "This isn't just about views or property values," one speaker said. "It's about who we are."

At the close of the three-hour hearing, the chair noted that nearly every speaker had used some version of the same phrase: that the project would "take away what makes this town this town." It is a concern, she said, that cannot be addressed by adjusting setbacks or lowering tower heights. It goes to the identity of the community itself.

In her remarks to the zoning board, Mrs. Halloran was plain: "You can mitigate noise, you can set back from property lines, but you cannot restore a community's sense of itself once it's gone. We will no longer be a farming town. We will be a host community for an industrial facility, and that is a different kind of place entirely."

The plan threatens a community character that cannot be measured in kilowatt-hours. Generations of families have farmed this valley, and the quiet rhythm of that life — the church bells, the county fair, the familiar horizon — is precisely what the project would destroy.

Letter to the editor, The Petoskey News-Review: The developers speak of megawatts and lease payments, but they say nothing of what we stand to lose. A rural township is more than its acreage. It is a way of life — neighbors who know one another, quiet evenings, a sense of continuity with those who came before. All of that is on the chopping block.

What is at stake here is not a view. It is the continuity of a community. Once you have imposed industrial infrastructure on a place that has never had it, the people who remain are no longer living in the same town. They are living in the ruins of it.

"They tell us we'll adjust," said longtime resident Bernard Kowalski at Thursday's forum. "But adjusting to something is not the same as keeping what you had. We had a community. We had our own way. We will not have that anymore, and no one on that panel seems to understand what that actually means to us."

From the submission of the Vinalhaven Concerned Citizens: An island community depends, perhaps more than any other, on a shared sense of character. When that character is overridden by outside developers with no stake in who we are, the community does not merely object — it begins to come apart.

From the minutes of the Prince Edward County council meeting: Councillor Ramsay stated that in his view the wind project represented "an existential threat to the character of the county" and that once the turbines were erected, "the Prince Edward County that our grandparents knew and that we promised our children would simply cease to exist."

The turbines are not merely tall structures. They are a declaration that this place is now something other than what it has been. The barn raisings, the volunteer fire suppers, the quiet Sundays — those things depend on a shared sense of place, and that sense of place does not survive industrialization of the skyline.

The opposition group argues that the cumulative effect of three approved projects — now totaling 87 turbines within a twelve-mile radius — has "effectively industrialized" a township that residents chose precisely for its rural, agricultural character, stripping it of the identity that drew most of them there in the first place.

Op-ed: Rural communities are not simply low-density populations. They are particular ways of life, with their own values, their own pace, their own sense of belonging. Large-scale wind development substitutes for that an impersonal industrial logic, and the community it finds is not the community it leaves behind.

What the developer calls "a modest footprint" is in fact the wholesale transformation of a community that has defined itself, for as long as anyone can remember, by the absence of industry. The turbines will not sit beside our community. They will replace it.

Letter to the Cattaraugus County Legislature: You are being told that a few turbines will not change much. But anyone who has lived here knows that our community is held together by something delicate — a shared way of seeing our own home. Disrupt that, and the community itself unravels.

Speaking to the Kiwanis Club in Clarion, the county commissioner put it plainly: "We have a maple syrup industry here. We have a hunting-camp industry. We have a hardwood-flooring industry and a Christmas-tree industry. I have yet to see a single wind developer explain to me how those industries will be better off — or even unchanged — after 80 turbines go up along the plateau."

Testimony submitted to the County Planning Commission, Exhibit 14: "The applicant's own socioeconomic study concedes that several traditional industries operating in the project footprint — including equestrian training facilities, specialty nurseries, and a regional film-location business — will experience measurable operational disruption. The study fails, however, to quantify the cascading effects on suppliers and service providers dependent on those primary industries."

At the podium, a soft-spoken man who identified himself as the third-generation owner of a regional trucking firm said the turbine transport permits issued last summer had "effectively shut down two of our lanes for six weeks." He added: "We lost a contract we'd held since 1998. The wind company got its blades delivered. A lot of industries around here got the bill."

"What the PUC does not seem to grasp," wrote the commissioner in her dissent, "is that the proposed surcharge does not merely raise household bills; it raises the operating costs of every energy-intensive industry in the state — foundries, paper mills, food processors, data centers, and cold-storage operators among them. These industries employ tens of thousands of our residents, and they are mobile."

Meeting notes, Appalachian Regional Commission workshop: Participants from several border counties described what one called "industry substitution at a loss" — rural economies trading a diversified base of agriculture, forestry, and recreation-tourism for a narrow dependence on wind-project payments to a small number of landowners. The consensus of the workshop was that this substitution should not be encouraged without rigorous industry-level impact analysis.

From a guest column in the Billings Gazette: Before we sign away another 200,000 acres to a Danish developer, perhaps we could ask which Montana industries this serves and which it displaces. Agriculture? Its practitioners are split and often unhappy. Tourism? The outfitters are lining up to oppose. Recreation? Ditto. At some point the list of losing industries becomes longer than the list of winning ones.

The Chamber of Commerce in our county has repeatedly warned that the proposed 340-megawatt wind development would impose burdens on a half-dozen local industries — from the dairy cooperatives that depend on uninterrupted access roads during calving season, to the small charter aviation outfits operating out of the regional airport, to the custom grain haulers whose oversized loads cannot share narrow shoulders with turbine transport convoys. These are not abstract concerns; they are the backbone of our rural economy.

According to a 2023 report commissioned by the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau and several allied trade groups, industrial wind development in the commonwealth's ridge-and-valley region has produced measurable negative effects on a number of established industries, and the report's authors caution that state incentive programs have systematically underweighted these losses in their cost-benefit analyses.

From the Nebraska Public Power District stakeholder comments: "Industrial customers in our service territory have expressed increasing concern that the pace and scale of intermittent generation build-out, combined with associated transmission cost allocations, is beginning to materially disadvantage industries that require firm, predictable power — particularly in the irrigation, food-processing, and manufacturing sectors."

Letter to the editor: I have farmed, trucked, and run a small equipment-repair shop in this valley for 41 years. What nobody in Topeka wants to admit is that when you carpet a working landscape with industrial turbines, you don't just displace one business — you disrupt a web of related industries that depended on that land being productive and accessible. Everyone from the crop-dusters to the feed suppliers takes a hit.

Op-ed, The Register-Guard: The governor's renewable portfolio standard is being sold as an economic engine, but the reality on the ground is that it is sand in the gears of several industries that were already doing just fine. Orchardists report interference with aerial spraying contractors. Vintners worry about microclimate shifts. Timber operators describe access-road conflicts with project haul routes. The "green economy" narrative papers over these real disruptions.

Minutes of the Regional Economic Development Authority, March board meeting: Members expressed concern that the proposed wind-lease auction area overlaps with sectors critical to the district's diversified economy. Staff was directed to prepare a report on potential adverse impacts to regional industries, including but not limited to agriculture, tourism, commercial recreation, and light manufacturing dependent on stable industrial power rates.

The problem with these sprawling renewable projects is that their proponents treat the rural economy as if it were empty space waiting to be "developed." It isn't. Every acre leased for turbines is an acre taken out of — or made more difficult for — some existing industry. That industry had workers, taxes, and a supply chain, and none of those costs show up in the developer's glossy brochure.

'This is not NIMBYism. This is the commanding general of Fort Riley telling us, in writing, that the project will harm his ability to train soldiers.' So said Geary County Commissioner Martha Peltz at a hearing last week, holding up a two-page letter from the installation's garrison commander opposing the Flint Hills wind expansion.

A Pentagon witness told the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee that 18 proposed wind projects currently under DoD review contain turbine siting that the department has assessed as presenting 'adverse' or 'substantial' impacts to military operations. 'Our concurrence rate looks high on paper,' the witness said, 'but that's because projects get modified or withdrawn once developers see what the impact analysis shows.'

During a tense town hall in Bowie County, a uniformed representative of Red River Army Depot told residents that the proposed Sulphur Fork wind project's turbine heights would interfere with the depot's ammunition demolition range safety arc. 'We cannot continue to certify the range as safe for its current mission if those towers go up where they're drawn on the map,' the officer said.

The Department of Defense's clearinghouse has flagged the proposed 230-turbine Cimarron Ridge project as presenting 'unmitigable impacts' to long-range radar coverage at Cannon Air Force Base. In a letter to the BLM, base commander Col. Raymond Hess wrote that the turbines' 650-foot blade tips would create persistent clutter within the installation's primary low-altitude training corridor, forcing pilots to reroute exercises that have been conducted from Cannon since 1958.

Hidalgo County commissioners heard from a Border Patrol Air and Marine Operations liaison who said proposed turbines along the Rio Grande corridor would force agency aircraft — which coordinate closely with DoD counter-narcotics missions — into higher and less effective surveillance altitudes, with downstream implications for joint task force operations.

At a public scoping meeting in Accomack County, retired Navy Capt. Doug Wren warned that the proposed wind array off the Delmarva coast would overlap a maritime corridor used for carrier strike group workups out of Norfolk. 'The fleet has precious few places left on the East Coast to rehearse,' Wren said. 'Each lease block we hand away is a workup our sailors won't get before deployment.'

In written comments submitted to NYSERDA, the commanding officer of Naval Weapons Station Earle objected to the routing of export cables for a proposed offshore wind facility, stating that the cable corridor would pass directly through a restricted anchorage used for munitions loading operations. 'The proposed alignment is incompatible with the continued execution of the station's national defense mission,' the letter stated.

The Camden County Board of Freeholders cited impacts to Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst's aerial refueling training tracks as a primary reason for voting down a zoning amendment that would have permitted commercial-scale wind turbines in the county's rural northern tier.

A white paper released by the Mitchell Institute warned that the current federal siting review process 'is structurally biased toward project approval' and does not adequately weight long-term readiness costs to the Department of Defense. The paper singled out wind development in the Southwest as a case study, arguing that several approved projects now constrain tactics development at Luke and Holloman.

The North Dakota Legislative Assembly's Interim Energy Committee heard testimony from a Minot AFB liaison officer who said proposed wind development in Ward and McHenry counties would intrude on low-level routes flown by B-52 crews and create radar returns that complicate ICBM security helicopter operations at missile alert facilities across the complex.

Pennsylvania state senator Rick Mastriano introduced a resolution urging the PJM Interconnection to account for military mission impacts in its generation interconnection queue, citing concerns raised by the 193rd Special Operations Wing at Harrisburg International Airport about proposed turbine development along its low-level ingress routes.

Huron County supervisors tabled a vote on the Thumb Breeze III expansion Monday night after receiving a letter from Selfridge Air National Guard Base expressing 'significant concern' that the additional turbines would further degrade training flight paths already constrained by prior phases of development. The letter, read aloud during the meeting, warned that any additional encroachment could jeopardize the base's future mission assignments under BRAC review.

In a rare public rebuke, the Navy's top Pacific airspace official said a proposed floating wind demonstration project off the central California coast would overlap Point Mugu Sea Range and 'meaningfully degrade our ability to conduct the weapons testing this nation relies on.' The statement was entered into the project's NEPA record.

Maine's congressional delegation has asked the Government Accountability Office to examine whether the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management adequately considered impacts to Naval Air Station Brunswick's successor training activities before advancing lease areas in the Gulf of Maine. 'The Navy's maritime patrol squadrons cannot be an afterthought in this process,' the delegation's joint letter stated.

'Every aviator I trained with at Whiting Field flew through airspace that is now, or soon will be, pockmarked with turbines from the Panhandle to South Alabama,' retired Cmdr. Jim Patterson wrote in an op-ed for the Pensacola News Journal. 'The Navy will adapt, because it has to. But make no mistake: we are asking young pilots to learn their craft in a smaller, more cluttered, more dangerous sky — and we are doing it to subsidize an industry that will not be there to defend this country when the time comes.'

Testimony before the House Armed Services Subcommittee on Readiness this week focused on what Rear Adm. (Ret.) Linda Caruthers described as 'a quiet but cumulative erosion of our test and training ranges' from offshore wind leases along the Atlantic coast. 'Every lease block granted inside the warning areas compresses the envelope our aviators have left to operate in,' she told members. 'You cannot reconstitute this airspace once it's built out.'

The Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project drew objections from the commanding officer of Naval Station Norfolk, who told federal regulators that turbine placements within the outer approaches to the Chesapeake Bay could complicate outbound transits of nuclear-powered vessels during degraded weather conditions. The objection was later resolved through a micrositing agreement, but has been cited by opponents of subsequent projects as evidence that military concerns are real and recurring.

A coalition of retired general officers has written to the Secretary of the Interior urging a pause on further lease sales in the Gulf of Mexico Call Area until a comprehensive mission compatibility assessment is completed for Eglin's overwater test ranges. The signatories warned that 'piecemeal project-by-project review has failed to capture the cumulative operational cost to the joint force.'

In comments filed with the Public Utility Commission of Texas, an attorney for a coalition of South Texas ranchers and retired military officers argued that the cumulative footprint of approved and pending wind projects has already 'materially degraded' Naval Air Station Kingsville's student jet training syllabus, and that additional development would 'render portions of the syllabus unexecutable within current airspace.'

A recent Congressional Research Service report noted that while the DoD Siting Clearinghouse has formally objected to only a small fraction of reviewed projects, internal service-level assessments reflect 'a substantially higher degree of concern' about cumulative wind development impacts on test ranges, special use airspace, and long-range radar systems — concerns that rarely translate into formal objections due to institutional pressure to concur.

Opponents of a proposed wind farm near Cavalier Air Force Station argued at a public hearing that the turbines would create radar clutter for the Perimeter Acquisition Radar, a key component of the nation's missile warning architecture. 'You are talking about degrading a sensor that watches for incoming ballistic threats,' one speaker told the commission. 'There is no local economic benefit that justifies that trade.'

Sen. Tommy Beaulieu (R-La.) has introduced legislation that would require any wind project within 100 miles of a military installation to obtain affirmative DoD concurrence before qualifying for federal tax credits. 'We've seen Fort Polk's aviators forced into ever-tighter boxes,' Beaulieu said in a floor speech. 'If the Pentagon says a project hurts readiness, the taxpayer should not be subsidizing that harm.'

Opponents of the Three Forks wind project told Jefferson County commissioners that the turbines would sit directly beneath a military operating area used by F-15s out of Kingsley Field. 'The Air National Guard has been flying that MOA since before most of us were born,' one resident said. 'One project, one time, and we lose it forever.'

A declassified summary of a 2023 Air Combat Command study, obtained through FOIA by the Center for Military Readiness, concluded that proposed wind development across seven counties in eastern Montana would reduce usable low-altitude training airspace at Malmstrom-associated ranges by an estimated 34 percent. The report characterized the cumulative impact as 'operationally significant.'

Local ranchers gathered outside the Val Verde County courthouse to support a county ordinance restricting industrial wind development within 30 miles of Laughlin Air Force Base. 'This isn't about the view,' said rancher Carl Hebert. 'Laughlin trains every Air Force pilot in the country. You put 600-foot towers under their pattern, you're telling the next generation of aviators to go train somewhere else — maybe somewhere that isn't in Texas.'

A guest column in the Charleston Gazette-Mail by former PSC commissioner Thomas Bayliss argues that West Virginia should pivot away from ridgetop wind development. "The Mountaineer and Beech Ridge projects have produced far less than promised while fragmenting some of our most sensitive ecosystems," Bayliss writes. "TerraPower and X-energy are both looking for host communities. A 300-megawatt advanced reactor at a retired coal site would employ more people at higher wages, generate firm power around the clock, and spare the ridges. That is the conversation Charleston should be having."

The Nebraska Public Power District board heard a presentation from consulting firm Harbinger Analytics on Tuesday. The firm's principal, Lee Whitaker, told directors that extending Cooper Nuclear Station's operating license to 80 years would preserve more annual clean generation than the district's entire 1,320 MW wind portfolio produces, at less than a third of the per-megawatt-hour cost. "If the board's charge is affordable, reliable, low-carbon power," Whitaker said, "the subsequent license renewal at Cooper is the highest-value decision in front of you. New wind contracts should take a back seat to that."

Excerpt from a speech by Finnish MEP Jukka Lehtinen at the European Parliament's ITRE committee: "Olkiluoto 3 was delayed and over budget — everyone knows this. It now produces more clean electricity in a year than the entire Finnish wind fleet, on a site you could fit inside a single wind lease area. Europe's obsession with wind while member states close reactors is not climate policy. It is climate theatre. Serious decarbonization means new build nuclear, extended operation of the existing fleet, and a clear-eyed view that wind cannot do this alone — or even mostly."

The Wyoming Public Service Commission heard testimony Tuesday from ratepayer advocate Douglas Merritt, who urged the panel to reject the Sweetwater Ridge wind proposal. "Per megawatt-hour delivered, the new AP1000 designs are coming in at roughly half the real cost of intermittent wind once you factor in the transmission build-out," Merritt said. "Nuclear runs 90-plus percent of the time. A nuclear license lasts 80 years. These turbines will be scrap metal in 20. If we're serious about dispatchable low-carbon power, the commission should direct resources toward the small modular reactor pilot at Kemmerer, not another ridgeline project."

Kansas state senator Wade Holloway, speaking to the Hutchinson Rotary Club: "I've voted against every wind tax abatement that's crossed my desk, and I'll tell you why. Wolf Creek generates more electricity in a month than the entire Flint Hills wind corridor generates in a year, and it does it without killing the viewshed or the bird population. We should be licensing two more units at Wolf Creek, not handing out ten-year abatements to offshore developers from Madrid."

A coalition of retired engineers calling itself Citizens for Sensible Power released a white paper Wednesday arguing that Minnesota's 2040 carbon-free mandate is achievable only through nuclear expansion. "Wind has had thirty years and billions in production tax credits and still cannot deliver baseload," the group's chair, Eleanor Vinck, told reporters outside the Capitol. "A gigawatt of nuclear on a few hundred acres does more for decarbonization than ten gigawatts of nameplate wind scattered across farm country. The legislature should lift the state's moratorium on new reactors before approving another turbine."

Excerpt from the Queensland Resources Council submission on the proposed Capricornia Wind Zone:

"The Council respectfully submits that the proposed 2.4 GW wind zone, even fully built, would deliver roughly 800 MW of average output. A single CANDU or AP1000 unit at an existing coastal site would deliver more firm capacity, occupy a fraction of the footprint, and avoid the biodiversity offset liabilities that are inevitable across the proposed corridor. Australia's prohibition on nuclear generation should be revisited before further wind zones are gazetted."

New Brunswick Energy Minister Kate Fournier, in a scrum with reporters: "Point Lepreau gives us 660 megawatts of clean, firm power every hour of every day. We're in serious conversations with ARC Clean Energy about siting advanced reactors here. I don't see how signing 25-year offtake agreements for Gulf of St. Lawrence wind makes sense when we can double down on a proven technology at Lepreau."

Dr. Meera Rajagopalan, professor of nuclear engineering at Purdue, speaking at an IEEE public forum last Thursday: "The honest comparison isn't wind versus coal. It's wind plus gas firming plus transmission plus storage versus nuclear. When you run that comparison on a consistent lifecycle basis, nuclear wins on land use, on materials intensity, on capacity factor, and increasingly on levelized cost once you include the system costs wind externalizes onto the rest of the grid."

Testimony of Dr. Harlan Pfeiffer before the Ohio Power Siting Board, Case No. 23-1184-EL-BGN:

"The applicant's own modeling shows the Black Fork wind facility will require natural gas firming for roughly 62 percent of operating hours. If the policy objective is low-carbon generation, a single AP300 reactor at the Davis-Besse site would displace more CO2 per dollar spent than the entire 380 megawatt nameplate proposed here, and would do so on less than two percent of the land. The board should weigh that opportunity cost when considering whether this project serves the public interest."

Letter to the Cornwall Standard-Freeholder:

I attended the open house for the proposed Raisin River wind project last week and left discouraged. The developer could not tell us the capacity factor with a straight face, could not explain what happens when the grid operator curtails them, and could not justify why Ontario should accept 180 of these things when Darlington is being refurbished to produce firm clean power for another generation. The answer to climate change is already running in Clarington. Build more of that.

— B. Séguin, Williamstown

Comment submitted to BOEM during the public comment period on the Central Atlantic Call Area (Docket BOEM-2023-0027):

"The agency's analysis fails to consider the opportunity cost of offshore wind relative to coastal nuclear deployment. The Surry and North Anna stations demonstrate that nuclear can deliver 1,000+ MW of firm, zero-carbon power at capacity factors north of 93 percent. Every dollar committed to a lease area with a 45 percent capacity factor and a 25-year asset life is a dollar not committed to reactors with 80-year lifespans. BOEM should coordinate with NRC on a comparative cost-per-tonne-avoided analysis before finalizing lease terms." — Submitted by J. Alderman, retired utility planner, Norfolk VA.

From a submitted comment on the Michigan Public Service Commission's Integrated Resource Plan docket:

"DTE's preferred portfolio leans heavily on 4,200 MW of new wind by 2035. The Commission should direct the utility to model a counterfactual portfolio in which Fermi 2 is relicensed and a Fermi 3 application is filed. Preliminary analysis by the intervenor suggests the nuclear-inclusive portfolio achieves the same 2035 emissions target with 38 percent less installed capacity, 60 percent less land, and a lower net present cost to ratepayers. Refusing to model that case because it is politically inconvenient is not sound resource planning."

Letter, The Daily Telegraph (UK):

Sir — Your columnist praises the latest round of Contracts for Difference for offshore wind. Might I suggest a different metric? Hinkley Point C, for all its difficulties, will deliver 3.2 GW of firm capacity for 60 years. Dogger Bank A, B and C combined will deliver a similar nameplate but with roughly half the annual output and a 25-year life. On a lifetime-terawatt-hour basis, the reactor is the better buy. The sooner Westminster acknowledges that, the sooner we stop chasing the wind around the North Sea.

Yours faithfully, G. Ashworth, Sevenoaks

A peer-reviewed modeling study by researchers at ETH Zürich, summarized in this week's Neue Zürcher Zeitung, finds that Switzerland's planned wind buildout would deliver only 2.1 TWh annually at 23 percent capacity factor, while extending the operating licenses of the Gösgen and Leibstadt reactors for another two decades would preserve roughly 17 TWh of firm low-carbon generation. The lead author, Prof. Weber, told NZZ: "The numbers make the tradeoff obvious. Closing the reactors to build wind is moving backward on decarbonization."

From the Aberdeen Press and Journal, opinion page:

The Scottish Government has committed Scotland to a pathway dominated by offshore wind, yet Torness and Hunterston B delivered decades of reliable, low-carbon electricity with a footprint you could walk across in an afternoon. The refusal to even discuss a replacement reactor at Torness is not a scientific position — it is an ideological one. Scots will pay for that ideology in constraint payments, grid upgrades, and imported gas every time the North Sea falls still.

During cross-examination at the Alberta Utilities Commission hearing on the Paintearth Wind Project, intervenor counsel Margaret Osei pressed the applicant's witness: "Would you agree that a CANDU refurbishment at Bruce delivered firming capacity at a capital cost per reliable megawatt well below what your project proposes?" The witness conceded the point on reliable megawatts but disputed the capital cost figure. Osei's closing submission argued the Commission should find that wind does not represent the least-cost pathway to emissions reduction where nuclear options remain available.

Board of Supervisors, Madison County VA, minutes of the October 14 meeting: Supervisor Critzer moved that the Board send a letter to the General Assembly opposing HB 2134's renewable-only procurement language. In discussion, Critzer stated, "We have North Anna right across the county line. It runs night and day. I don't understand why the state won't count that as clean. If we want clean power we should be building another reactor, not contracting for wind from Wise County that we can't count on in August." Motion carried 5-1.

Rep. Caldwell (R-TX-19), floor statement: "Mr. Speaker, my colleagues on the other side keep telling rural Texans that turbines are the answer. I represent ranchers whose neighbors leased land fifteen years ago and are now stuck with non-operating machines and no decommissioning fund. Meanwhile, the reactors at Comanche Peak have quietly generated clean power for three decades. If we were honest about carbon and honest about cost, we would be expediting licenses for advanced reactors, not extending the wind PTC for a fifth time."

During Monday's county board meeting, Supervisor Haines pushed back on the developer's presentation. "You're asking us to lease 14,000 acres for a project with a 34 percent capacity factor. The Vogtle units in Georgia, for all their cost overruns, will still produce more firm energy on 3,000 acres than this sprawl ever will. Why are we not having a serious conversation about hosting a small reactor instead?"

Op-ed, The Arizona Republic, by former APS engineer Daniel Escárcega:

Palo Verde, 40 miles west of Phoenix, is the largest power plant in the United States. It has run for four decades with a capacity factor above 90 percent and emits no carbon. Yet the Corporation Commission keeps approving wind contracts from New Mexico that deliver a third of their nameplate and require hundreds of miles of new transmission. The math is not difficult. A second Palo Verde — or a cluster of small modular reactors on the same site — would decarbonize Arizona faster and cheaper than any amount of imported wind.

Ontario Premier's remarks at the Bruce County Chamber luncheon, as reported by the Kincardine Record: "Look, the Bruce refurbishment is going to give this province clean power for another fifty years at a levelized cost well below what the offshore wind proponents are quoting. I've said it before — if you want emissions down and bills stable, you build out the reactor fleet. You don't paper the escarpment with 180-metre towers."

Letter to the editor — The Albany Times Union

Your editorial page continues to cheerlead for offshore wind as though no alternative exists. France gets roughly 70 percent of its electricity from reactors, and its emissions per kilowatt-hour are a fraction of Germany's. Germany, meanwhile, shuttered its last reactors and now burns lignite when the North Sea goes calm. If Governor Hochul genuinely wants clean, reliable power for downstate load centers, she should champion advanced reactors at the Nine Mile Point site, not gamble the grid on turbines that only spin a third of the time.

R. Coughlin, Delmar

Statement issued by the Citizens' Nuclear Advocacy Network following the Department of Energy's announcement of $1.1 billion in offshore wind transmission grants:

"The Department continues to direct scarce federal dollars toward a generation technology that cannot, by its physics, provide firm capacity. The same $1.1 billion applied to the advanced reactor demonstration program would accelerate deployment of designs that deliver 24/7 carbon-free electricity with a footprint and materials intensity an order of magnitude below offshore wind. CNAN calls on Congress to rebalance the clean energy portfolio toward the only proven, scalable, firm low-carbon resource: nuclear fission."

When the polar vortex hit the Midwest last January, it wasn't the wind fleet that kept the lights on—it was the coal plants MISO has been trying to retire. Gas and coal units ran at nearly full capacity while wind output collapsed to under 4% of nameplate. The lesson is obvious to anyone willing to learn it: dispatchable thermal generation is not a relic, it is the reason your furnace kept running. You cannot responsibly shutter those assets on the promise that a turbine somewhere in Iowa will spin on demand.

The Montana Public Service Commission heard testimony yesterday that Colstrip Unit 4 had outperformed the state's entire wind fleet on availability for the twelfth consecutive quarter. "Coal just works," said commissioner Daines. "It doesn't need the wind to blow or the sun to shine. At some point we have to stop apologizing for assets that have delivered exactly what they were built to deliver."

Chairman Whitaker opened the hearing by noting that during the February cold event, the Cumberland Fossil Plant generated more electricity in 72 hours than the state's entire wind fleet had produced in the preceding month. "I'm not opposed to new technology," he said. "I'm opposed to pretending that a technology which failed when we needed it most is ready to replace the one that didn't."

The ERCOT post-mortem from Winter Storm Uri made one thing clear, even if the authors buried it: gas generation carried Texas through the worst of the freeze. Wind collapsed to a fraction of its forecasted output precisely when demand peaked. No honest engineer looks at those numbers and concludes we need more turbines. We need more firm thermal capacity, and we need to stop pretending the two are interchangeable.

A reader writes: I spent thirty years as a plant operator at a coal-fired station in Indiana. When we ran, we ran—rain, snow, heat dome, ice storm. The turbines that replaced us sit idle more days than they spin. Anyone who tells you wind is a substitute for what we did has never stood in a control room at 3 a.m. during a January blackout warning, waiting for the system operator to tell you to push output to 105%.

The Heartland Reliability Study, released quietly last month, found that states with higher wind penetration have not decarbonized faster than states that invested in combined-cycle gas. If anything, the gas-heavy states posted larger absolute emissions reductions at a fraction of the ratepayer cost. The implication is uncomfortable for the wind lobby but unavoidable: the cheapest and most reliable path away from coal runs through natural gas, not through a forest of turbines.

There's a reason the Chinese, who lecture the West on climate ambition, opened more than 70 gigawatts of new coal capacity last year while building turbines for export. They understand what our political class refuses to acknowledge: coal is dense, storable, and dispatchable. Wind is none of those things. A country serious about industrial competitiveness builds its grid on the first and sells the second to the credulous.

Dr. Feldman's testimony cut through the rhetoric: "The capacity factor data is unambiguous. Wind delivers roughly 35% of nameplate on a good year in the best locations. Natural gas combined-cycle delivers above 85% and can be dispatched on demand. If you are serious about reliable, affordable electricity, you build more of the latter and stop pretending the former is equivalent."

Op-ed, Casper Star-Tribune: Wyoming coal built this state. It funded our schools, our roads, our hospitals. Now Washington wants us to trade that inheritance for a crop of turbines owned by a Spanish conglomerate and financed by tax credits paid for by taxpayers in states that will never see a single blade. I'll take the Jim Bridger Plant any day. It runs 24 hours, employs our neighbors, and doesn't need the weather to cooperate.

The delusion at the heart of the net-zero movement is the idea that intermittent sources can displace the hydrocarbon economy. They cannot. Germany has spent nearly half a trillion euros on its Energiewende and still burns lignite—the dirtiest coal on earth—to keep its factories running when the North Sea goes still. If the greenest country in Europe cannot wind its way off fossil fuels after two decades of trying, the rest of us should stop pretending we will.

Public comment, Otsego County Planning Board, March 14: I've lived here forty-one years. The natural gas line that runs through this township has never once failed us. It heats our homes in January, it runs the school, it keeps the hospital open. Now you're asking us to accept 600-foot turbines on the ridgeline so that somewhere down the road—nobody can say when—that reliable gas might be switched off. That's not an upgrade. That's a downgrade dressed up in green paint.

Guest column, Bismarck Tribune: Lignite coal from the Center Mine has powered North Dakota homes reliably for three generations. Now the Coyote Station is slated for closure so the utility can meet a renewable target set by regulators who've never wintered here. The math doesn't work. The engineering doesn't work. And when the January wind dies and the thermometer hits forty below, it won't be a wind turbine that keeps your pipes from freezing. It'll be the plant they're tearing down.

Letter to the editor: The county commission's enthusiasm for the Prairie Ridge wind project ignores a simple fact. My cousin farms near a wind development in Kansas and tells me the diesel generators on site run more often than the turbines produce useful power. Meanwhile, the shuttered coal plant outside Emporia employed 240 people and delivered electricity at a fraction of what ratepayers pay now. We are trading something that worked for something that doesn't, and pretending it's progress.

It is worth remembering that every kilowatt-hour of wind electricity sold in this country is sold into a market that depends on natural gas to function. When the turbines feather, gas ramps. When the turbines spin too hard, gas curtails. The wind industry is not a competitor to gas—it is a dependent. Strip away the production tax credit and the renewable portfolio standard and the honest arrangement would reveal itself: gas generates the electricity, and wind collects the subsidy.

Senator McCallister was blunt during Tuesday's floor debate. "The notion that we can rid the world of coal and gas by planting turbines from here to the Pacific is a fantasy peddled by people who have never had to meet a payroll or keep a hospital's emergency generators fueled. Fossil fuels built modernity. Wind, for all the billions thrown at it, has not retired a single baseload plant that wasn't shut down by fiat."

Any honest accounting concludes the same thing: the cheapest, most reliable molecule ever discovered for generating electricity at scale is methane, and the most reliable solid fuel remains coal. The wind industry has spent three decades and a trillion global dollars trying to dethrone them and has not succeeded. At some point, persistence in the face of repeated failure stops being ambition and starts being folly.

The hard truth the Commonwealth's energy plan avoids is that every retirement of a dispatchable fossil asset has been followed by a deterioration in grid reliability metrics. NERC has flagged it. PJM has flagged it. The operators who actually run the system are telling anyone who will listen that coal and gas are not optional, and that wind—however much we build—is not a substitute. The plan persists anyway because the politics demand it, not because the engineering supports it.

Statement from the Roscommon County Farm Bureau: Our members have watched neighboring counties approve wind projects and seen the results. Diesel generators trucked in to power substations when the wind dies. Propane bills rising because gas infrastructure gets deprioritized. The simple truth is that the reliable, affordable energy our dairy operations depend on is natural gas, and any policy that sacrifices gas on the altar of wind will put working farms out of business.

Rep. Harriman told the committee that the state's experiment with wind had produced "exactly the opposite of what was advertised." He noted that every megawatt of nameplate wind capacity added since 2015 had been shadowed by a corresponding increase in natural gas peaking capacity. "We didn't replace anything," he said. "We built two grids and handed the bill to ratepayers. If the goal had been cheap, reliable electricity, we would have kept the combined-cycle plant at Ridgeway open and called it a day."

The Cooperative Rural Electric Association has warned members that the proposed retirement of the Thornburg gas peakers would leave the service territory dependent on wind output during peak winter hours—a prospect the Association's chief engineer called "indefensible." In a letter to the board, she noted that the gas units had operated at 94% availability over the last decade and recommended members vote against the transition plan.

Mr. Dolinsky told the select committee that the proposed closure of the Nanticoke backup gas units was premature. "We watched Alberta last winter. Their grid operator issued emergency alerts because wind dropped to under 2% of capacity during a cold snap. The only reason the province didn't black out was natural gas peaking. Ontario would be reckless to follow a path that Alberta is already regretting."

Commercial fishermen from three ports testified that the lease area overlaps the most productive scallop grounds on the shelf. "Move it twenty miles east into deeper water and you'd hear nothing from us," said one captain. "But they picked the one square they shouldn't have picked."

"You can call it NIMBY if you want," the homeowner association president said, "but the state's siting guidelines exist for a reason, and this project violates four of them. That's not NIMBYism. That's the rules."

The Highlands Coalition's written submission argues the developer selected the Beaver Creek ridge not because it is the best wind resource in the region — it isn't — but because the landowner was willing. "Siting decisions driven by lease availability rather than suitability are exactly how we end up with projects in the wrong places."

"We told them three years ago the Meadowbrook parcel was the wrong place," said Karen Oltmans of Neighbors for Responsible Siting. "It floods. It's next to the hospital helipad. And it's surrounded by homes on three sides. They ignored all of it and filed the permit anyway."

Residents of the Elk Ridge subdivision filed a joint letter with the Public Utilities Commission objecting to the Summit Pass project, arguing the ridgeline chosen is among the most visible in the county and that a lower-elevation parcel to the east — owned by the same developer — would achieve comparable wind speeds without dominating the skyline from every home in a four-mile radius.

Letter to the editor: Has anyone at the zoning board actually driven Route 9 at dusk? The turbines they're proposing would be less than a half mile from the elementary school and directly behind the veterans' cemetery. You could not pick a worse spot in the entire township if you tried.

Chairman Whitaker read from the staff report: the proposed turbine locations fall within 300 meters of two identified Archaic-period sites and cross a parcel the tribal historic preservation office has repeatedly asked to be excluded from industrial development. The project as submitted, he said, cannot be approved at this location.

Public comment, Deborah Klassen: I grew up on this road. The turbines they want to build would be closer to our well than the highway is. Put them somewhere that isn't on top of a drinking water recharge zone.

The Audubon chapter does not oppose wind energy in principle, its president told commissioners, but "siting a 78-turbine array across a documented golden eagle foraging ground, when the state's own mapping tool flags this exact section as high-risk, is simply indefensible. There are better places."

"There is nothing wrong with wind power," Councillor Aarav Mehta said. "There is something very wrong with building it in the middle of a community that has said no three times and which the developer's own noise model shows will exceed the nighttime limit at eleven receptors."

Dr. Helena Voss, a landscape ecologist who reviewed the application at the town's request, concluded the developer's site selection methodology was "backwards" — beginning with willing landowners rather than with an environmental constraints map. "If you start the other way around," she wrote, "this ridge is not in the top twenty candidate sites in the county."

Testimony from the regional emergency management coordinator: the proposed turbine string runs parallel to the medevac flight path serving two rural hospitals. Relocation of the array south of the county road would eliminate the conflict entirely. The developer has declined to consider it.

The town's comprehensive plan, updated in 2021, designates the northern escarpment as a conservation overlay. The applicant's decision to site 14 turbines inside that overlay — rather than on the industrial-zoned flats six miles south — has drawn unanimous opposition from the planning board.

"You can't put 600-foot machines 1,200 feet from a farmhouse and call that responsible planning," said county supervisor Marlene Doherty at Tuesday's hearing. "Every other jurisdiction in the region uses a one-mile setback. Pick a location that respects the people who actually live there."

Planning officer's recommendation: refuse. The application site lies within the designated Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty and directly adjoins a scheduled monument. The applicant has not demonstrated why sites outside the AONB were not pursued.

The Heritage Commission's formal objection focuses on viewshed impacts to the 18th-century stone churches along the valley floor. The commission notes that a ridge 12 km to the west, outside any heritage-sensitive corridor, was identified as a superior wind resource in the developer's own feasibility scoping but was set aside for reasons never disclosed to the public.

Mayor Jürgen Halverson was blunt at the press conference: "The developer wants to put 22 turbines between the school, the hospital, and the nature reserve. There are three other sites in this municipality where the same capacity could be built with none of those conflicts. Until they explain why they chose the worst one, the answer from this town is no."

"This is prime Class I farmland," the county Farm Bureau president told the committee. "You don't put an industrial wind facility on the best soil in the state when there are thousands of acres of marginal ground ten miles north that would host the same project without taking food production offline."

Opponents of the offshore proposal note that the wind lease was drawn up before the federal survey identifying the area as critical habitat for the North Atlantic right whale was finalized. "The lease boundary needs to move," said the coalition spokesperson. "It was drawn in the wrong place and everyone now knows it."

The village council voted 6-1 to oppose the project on siting grounds alone, citing proximity to the regional airport's approach corridor, the historic district boundary, and an active peregrine nesting cliff within 800 meters of the nearest proposed tower.

The proposed 42-turbine project sits directly on the migratory corridor identified in the state's 2019 wildlife atlas. Selectmen have asked the developer to explain why no alternative site on the adjacent plateau — already cleared and closer to existing transmission — was evaluated in the siting report submitted to the commission.

Letter from the Lake Association: our members do not object to wind development in the county. We object to this wind development, on this shoreline, within view of every dock and every cottage, when the interior uplands offer comparable wind and no visual conflict with a recreational resource that supports hundreds of local businesses.

The fiscal note attached to HB 2241 assumes that utility-scale wind will generate net-positive revenue for host counties. That assumption collapses under scrutiny. Once you subtract the statutory property tax exemption for renewable generation equipment, the abatements negotiated project-by-project, and the offsetting loss of agricultural assessment on enrolled parcels, most host counties in the three case studies reviewed ran a revenue deficit in years one through seven.

Rural school districts have been the quiet losers in the wind rush. In three of the four districts we surveyed in the western part of the state, the expected tax windfall from turbine construction was partially or entirely offset by reductions in state aid, which is calibrated to local property wealth. The turbines raised the district's assessed value on paper, the state reduced its contribution accordingly, and the negotiated PILOT meant the district never actually saw the full assessed revenue.

What is often lost in the debate is that the host municipality does not simply fail to gain revenue; it affirmatively loses revenue relative to the prior agricultural use, because the PILOT replaces both the farmland assessment and any potential commercial assessment. Land that was generating $4,200 a year in property tax under Ag Use now generates $3,100 under the PILOT. That is a negative delta, not a neutral one.

Township Trustee Dan Kowalski noted at Monday's meeting that the access roads built to accommodate turbine components have already required $180,000 in unplanned maintenance, a figure not contemplated in the host community agreement. "The agreement pays us roughly $42,000 a year," Kowalski said. "We are running a deficit on this project and the blades haven't even started turning on half the units yet."

The promise of millions in new tax revenue has been the centerpiece of every wind proposal I have seen in this county over the past decade. The reality, once the abatements, the PILOTs, the equipment exemptions, and the depreciation schedules are accounted for, is a fraction of that headline number. Residents deserve the net figure, not the gross.

The PILOT agreement before the town board is a bad deal for Chautauqua County taxpayers. Under the proposed structure, Pattern Energy would pay $8,500 per megawatt for 20 years, a rate substantially below what the turbines would generate under standard assessed value. That shortfall has to be made up somewhere, and it will be made up by homeowners and small businesses through higher property tax bills. The school district, which depends on stable revenue, will see per-pupil funding erode at precisely the moment enrollment is rising.

The municipal finance literature on wind PILOTs is surprisingly thin, but the case studies that do exist — DeKalb County, Illinois; Somerset County, Maryland; Huron County, Michigan — converge on a common finding. Host jurisdictions systematically overestimate the revenue yield of negotiated tax agreements in the first decade and underestimate the offsetting infrastructure and administrative costs.

Councilwoman Ortega pressed the developer's representative on the decommissioning bond. "If this company is sold, or goes bankrupt in year fifteen, and the bond turns out to be insufficient, who removes these turbines?" The representative acknowledged that, absent adequate bonding, the obligation would fall to the landowner or, failing that, to the county. Ortega's point was straightforward: taxpayers should not be the insurer of last resort for a private commercial venture.

At a cost of roughly $4.7 million per mile, the transmission spur required to connect the proposed facility to the regional grid will be paid for through a rate-base adjustment, but the associated easement acquisitions, road right-of-way modifications, and emergency-response capacity upgrades will be borne by the host counties. None of those costs appear in the developer's economic impact brochure.

Residents of Somerset Township should not be misled by the developer's talking points about "tens of millions in local tax revenue." That number is the gross figure over the 25-year project life, undiscounted, and assumes no further abatements. The net present value to the township, after the host community agreement discounts and the state equipment exemption, is closer to $2.1 million — and a substantial portion of that is offset by road and emergency-service costs the township will incur.

Letter to the editor: My property taxes went up 9 percent this year. The wind farm the board approved three years ago, which was supposed to lower our tax burden, is generating less than half the revenue the developer promised. I attended every meeting. I asked the questions. I was told I didn't understand the economics. It turns out I understood them quite well.

It should concern every taxpayer in this district that the developer negotiated a confidentiality clause into the host community agreement, preventing the township from disclosing the specific payment terms. Public money — or, more precisely, forgone public revenue — is at stake. The secrecy is not incidental. It is structural, and it prevents residents from evaluating whether their local government got a fair deal.

The host community agreement, as drafted, exempts the developer from the local road use impact fee that every other commercial hauler in this township pays. That exemption alone, based on the projected truck traffic during the 14-month construction period, represents roughly $340,000 in forgone revenue — revenue that would have offset the road damage the same trucks are causing.

The fiscal impact analysis that the state Public Service Commission relied upon to approve the Heritage Wind project assumed a 2.1 percent annual growth in host community payments. The executed agreement contains no such escalator. The commissioners should explain how a flawed assumption of that magnitude made it into the record without challenge, and whether the host community can now petition for reconsideration given the revenue shortfall.

Supervisor Hensley told the room what everyone already suspected: if the Blue Ridge wind project goes through under the current terms, the township will be collecting roughly one-third of the tax revenue it would collect from a comparable commercial development of the same footprint. "We are being asked to host the infrastructure, absorb the road damage, and accept a discount rate on the taxes," he said. "That is not a partnership. That is a subsidy from us to them."

Dear Editor: Before the council votes next Tuesday, residents should ask one simple question. Who pays for the new substation access road, the culvert replacements on County Route 19, and the bridge reinforcement the developer's own engineering report says will be necessary? The answer, buried on page 47 of the application, is the county highway department. That means us.

The auditor's report released this month shows that Kossuth County's general fund received $612,000 less in 2023 from the MidAmerican wind project than the original 2015 projections anticipated. The shortfall is attributed to a combination of accelerated depreciation, a downward equipment reassessment, and a renegotiated PILOT that was quietly approved by the prior board.

The town budget for fiscal year 2025 shows an increased levy on residential parcels to cover the gap left by the wind project's expired abatement-plus-PILOT structure, which was replaced with a lower renewable energy equipment valuation under the state statute passed last session. In plain terms: the developer's tax bill went down, and yours went up. That is not an accident of drafting; it is the intended consequence of the legislation the wind lobby spent three years writing.

It is worth reminding readers that when a wind project receives a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes arrangement, the county gives up its ability to reassess the property as the equipment depreciates or as market conditions change. In effect, the municipality locks itself into a twenty-year contract with no exit clause. Riverside County learned this lesson the hard way when its 1980s-era turbines were abandoned and the cleanup costs fell to local government.

Commissioner Vance asked the obvious question at last week's hearing: if the wind company's projections of property tax revenue are so reliable, why is the company unwilling to guarantee a revenue floor? The developer's counsel declined to commit, which told the commission everything it needed to know about where the downside risk actually sits.

County Assessor Marguerite Chen's testimony was unambiguous: "When a wind project comes in under a state equipment exemption, the assessor's office has no authority to include the turbines in the tax base. The only revenue the county receives is whatever the developer voluntarily negotiates. That is not taxation. That is charity, and the developer sets the terms."

When Iberdrola negotiated its tax stabilization agreement with the town, the town's bargaining position was weak because the alternative — litigating the assessment — would have cost the town more than the difference in tax yield. That is the dynamic at work in nearly every host community. The developer has national counsel and unlimited time. The town has a part-time attorney and a volunteer board. The revenue shortfall is baked into that asymmetry.

A point that deserves more attention: the federal production tax credit flows to the developer, but the infrastructure burdens — road wear, emergency services capacity, siting enforcement — flow to the county. The vertical mismatch means state and local taxpayers underwrite a project whose primary financial benefits are captured at the federal corporate level and by the out-of-state owner.

The town's bond counsel warned the board, in writing, that entering a 20-year PILOT without an escalator clause tied to inflation would expose the town to significant erosion of real revenue over the life of the agreement. The board approved the agreement anyway. At current inflation rates, the nominal $195,000 annual payment will be worth approximately $118,000 in 2044 dollars.

Members of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe told state regulators Tuesday that a proposed transmission corridor tied to a 500 MW wind development would cross lands containing unmarked burials and ceremonial grounds. "We were not consulted until the route was already drawn," said tribal historic preservation officer Marlene Iron Cloud. "That is not consultation. That is notification."

The Aroostook Band of Micmacs has joined neighboring Wabanaki nations in opposing a proposed wind corridor in northern Maine, citing impacts on moose habitat central to traditional subsistence hunting. Tribal council member Richard Silliboy said developers have treated consultation as "a box to check" rather than a genuine exchange. "Our relationship with the land predates the state of Maine," he said.

The Gwich'in Steering Committee has expressed concern about a proposed wind and hybrid energy development near caribou calving routes in interior Alaska, warning that any disturbance to the Porcupine herd carries consequences that extend far beyond project boundaries. "Our food, our ceremonies, our songs all come from the caribou," said committee chair Bernadette Demientieff. "A project that endangers them endangers us."

The Navajo Nation Council passed a resolution this week opposing a proposed 200-turbine project near Black Mesa, citing concerns that the development would disrupt ceremonial sites and access to plants used in traditional medicine. "Our elders have gathered here for generations," said Delegate Harriet Begay. "This is not empty land. It is a living part of who we are."

The Lenca communities of La Paz, Honduras, continue to resist a wind expansion proposed along the ridgelines above their villages. Leaders point to the 2016 assassination of environmental defender Berta Cáceres as a warning sign that has gone unheeded. "Every project comes wrapped in promises of development," said community spokesperson Pascuala Vásquez. "What arrives is division, intimidation, and the loss of our rivers and hills."

The Yaqui communities along the Río Yaqui in Sonora have opposed a wind and transmission project they say was approved without the prior consultation guaranteed to them under Mexican law. "The government speaks of a just energy transition," said traditional authority Guadalupe Flores. "For us, there is nothing just about a project that arrives already permitted."

The Kumeyaay Nation has long opposed wind development in the mountains east of San Diego, where tribal members say turbine construction on Campo and nearby lands has damaged archaeological features and interfered with traditional gathering. "They dynamited a ridge where our ancestors walked," tribal historian Michael Connolly Miskwish told the county planning commission. "No amount of lease revenue makes that right."

First Nations leaders in Ontario have raised concerns about a proposed wind project on Manitoulin Island, noting that environmental assessments failed to address impacts on fish weirs and portage routes still used by Anishinaabe community members. "The province keeps telling us we were consulted," said Chief Patsy Corbiere. "Receiving a letter in the mail is not consultation under our treaty relationship."

In Oaxaca's Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Zapotec and Ikoots communities have spent more than a decade pushing back against the cluster of wind parks that now dominate the landscape. Residents of San Dionisio del Mar say developers negotiated leases with a handful of ejido officials, bypassing the community assembly process required under their usos y costumbres. "They came with engineers and lawyers and left with signatures from people who did not speak for us," said fisherman Alberto Ruiz.

The Penobscot Nation has asked Maine regulators to halt a permit review for a ridge-top wind project pending a full assessment of impacts to Katahdin viewsheds and associated cultural values. "Katahdin is not scenery to us," tribal ambassador Maulian Bryant told the commission. "It is a relative. You are being asked to permit turbines on the skyline of a relative."

The Ngäbe-Buglé in western Panama have opposed a proposed wind corridor that would run through their comarca, arguing the state approved preliminary studies without engaging the traditional congress. Community organizer Silvia Carrera said the project fits a pattern of energy development imposed on indigenous lands. "First the dams, now the turbines," she said. "Always our territory. Never our decision."

The Wayuu of La Guajira, Colombia, have staged multiple road blockades against a cluster of wind projects advancing through their ancestral territory. Community leaders say prior consultation processes have been reduced to information sessions, with agreements signed by individuals who lack standing under Wayuu customary law. "The wind belongs to Juya," said one authority from Jepirachi. "It is not a commodity for companies to sell in Bogotá."

Members of the Osage Minerals Council told a federal judge last month that the continued operation of the Osage Wind facility on their reservation constitutes an ongoing trespass on mineral estate held in trust for the Nation. The case, which the tribe has pursued for more than a decade, highlights deeper frustrations about wind siting on or near reservation lands without meaningful tribal consent.

The Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation submitted comments objecting to a large wind proposal in the Columbia Plateau, noting that the project area overlaps ceded lands where the Tribes retain treaty-reserved rights to hunt, fish, and gather. The comments criticized the lead agency for framing consultation as optional rather than as a trust obligation.

Indigenous Masai communities in Kajiado, Kenya, have raised objections to the Kipeto wind project's expansion, arguing that grazing access promised during initial negotiations has been eroded by fencing and access-road restrictions. Elders told a county public hearing that younger herders are being pushed toward urban migration as seasonal routes close off.

In a letter to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, the Shinnecock Indian Nation raised objections to the siting of export cables for a planned offshore wind lease area off Long Island, noting that the proposed landing point crosses a known ancestral village site. The letter requests a full Section 106 review and a government-to-government consultation that the Nation says has not yet occurred.

The Mashpee Wampanoag and Aquinnah Wampanoag tribes have continued to raise concerns about offshore wind lease areas in Nantucket Sound and adjacent waters, arguing that turbine arrays interrupt unobstructed sightlines to the eastern horizon that are essential to sunrise ceremonies. Tribal council members say federal reviews have acknowledged the issue on paper but have not materially altered the siting of proposed projects.

In Norway's Fosen peninsula, Sámi reindeer herders won a 2021 Supreme Court ruling declaring that two wind farms built on their grazing lands violated their rights under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Years later, the turbines still turn. Young Sámi activists have repeatedly occupied government ministries in Oslo, demanding the state comply with its own highest court.

Aboriginal traditional owners in the Eyre Peninsula of South Australia have lodged objections to a proposed wind farm that would be built across a songline running through their country. Barngarla representatives told the state planning panel that the developer's cultural heritage survey relied on desktop records rather than on-country consultation with elders, and they called for the assessment to be redone.

A Sámi reindeer herding cooperative in northern Sweden has filed a fresh complaint with the Supreme Court after the Markbygden wind development continued to expand into traditional grazing corridors. Herders testified that the turbines scatter reindeer during migration and that compensation offers have not addressed the long-term loss of winter pasture. The complaint argues the project violates the cooperative's rights under ILO Convention 169, which Sweden has yet to ratify.

In Taiwan, Paiwan and Amis community members have protested onshore wind development near coastal villages, arguing that developers and the Bureau of Energy treat tribal consent as advisory rather than binding. A joint statement from several community associations called for the revision of the Indigenous Peoples Basic Law's consultation provisions, which they say are routinely circumvented by project proponents.

A coalition of Pueblo governors in New Mexico submitted joint testimony opposing a wind and transmission project proposed on lands adjacent to Chaco Canyon. The governors warned that the development would damage the broader cultural landscape recognized by UNESCO and that federal agencies had not adequately weighed impacts on ancestral sites located outside the park boundary.

The carbon footprint of manufacturing a single offshore turbine — the steel monopile, the tower sections shipped from Korea, the nacelle from Denmark, the blades from Spain, the installation vessels burning marine diesel — is staggering. Add to that the fact that none of the composite components can be recycled and you are looking at an industry that produces pollution at both ends of the lifecycle and pretends otherwise.

Letter: I used to believe the pitch. Then I toured a decommissioning site outside Lubbock and saw the trenches where they bury the blades — just trenches, filled with fiberglass, covered over, forgotten. It looked like a landfill. It was a landfill. I do not know how anyone can look at that and call it green.

A recent report from the Energy and Policy Institute of Finland found that blade waste from onshore wind is projected to exceed 43 million tonnes globally by 2050. There is currently no commercially viable recycling pathway for thermoset composites. The industry's answer has been to grind them into road filler or bury them, which is not a solution but an externality being passed to future generations.

Op-ed: When the turbines in Palm Springs started coming down in the late 2010s, residents discovered that leaking transformer oil had contaminated soils well beyond the pad footprint. The cleanup was never fully completed. This is the reality of wind's lifecycle, and it is coming to rural communities across the Midwest whether we like it or not.

A study out of the Technical University of Denmark last year found measurable concentrations of bisphenol-based epoxy particulates in surface waters downwind of large turbine arrays. The industry response was to commission its own study. This is the pattern: harm documented, harm denied, harm externalized.

The uncomfortable truth about the so-called green revolution is that every 2.5 MW turbine requires roughly 150 tonnes of steel, 4.7 tonnes of copper, and a nacelle stuffed with rare earths ripped out of Inner Mongolian tailings ponds. When these machines reach end of life in 20 years, the fiberglass blades can't be recycled and are either buried whole in landfills in Casper, Wyoming, or shipped overseas to become somebody else's problem.

There is a reason the industry does not want to talk about end-of-life. Because end-of-life is a dump truck full of toxic composite rolling into a rural landfill that was never designed to accept it, and a foundation of concrete and rebar left in the ground forever, and a pad of compacted subsoil that will not grow anything for a generation.

The province's own environmental assessment acknowledged that each turbine foundation would permanently displace approximately 1,200 cubic metres of soil and aggregate, and that the concrete and rebar would remain in place in perpetuity. In what universe is pouring a thousand permanent concrete plugs across prime agricultural land described as environmentally friendly?

Wind proponents love to wave around the word sustainable, but there is nothing sustainable about a machine that requires 900 pounds of neodymium per turbine, most of it refined in Baotou where the radioactive sludge lakes are visible from space. Every blade, every magnet, every gearbox is a downstream pollution event someone else has to live with.

Wind turbines are not clean. They leak. They shed. They erode. They require constant lubrication with oils that inevitably make their way into the surrounding soil, and when they fail — and they do fail — the cleanup falls on whoever happens to own the land underneath.

Submission to the County Board: The proposed facility will generate an estimated 18,000 tonnes of non-recyclable composite waste over its operational lifetime. The applicant has not identified a disposal facility, has not posted financial assurance adequate to the task, and has not addressed the PFAS and bisphenol leaching concerns raised by our county health officer. This project should not proceed until these questions are answered.

The claim that wind is zero-emission is marketing, not science. A lifecycle analysis that honestly accounts for mining, refining, transport, construction, maintenance, and disposal produces a very different number — and that number gets worse every time a blade ends up in a ditch or a nacelle catches fire in Kansas.

Testimony, Public Service Commission hearing: I asked the developer's representative three times what would happen to the blades at end of life, and three times he said we're working on solutions. That is not an answer. That is an admission that there is no answer.

Offshore turbines are worse. The sacrificial anodes slough aluminum and zinc into the water column year after year. The antifouling coatings leach biocides. The subsea cables release SF6 when they fail. And when the foundations are finally pulled — if they are pulled — the disturbance plume of heavy metals and sediment is a multi-square-kilometre event nobody has adequately modeled.

The sustainability story collapses the moment you follow the supply chain. Lithium from Atacama brine fields draining indigenous water tables. Balsa wood from Ecuadorian forests clear-cut for blade cores. Rare earths from Jiangxi tailings. Steel from coal-fired Chinese mills.
