Every component of a wind turbine is somebody else's environmental catastrophe, and we are told to celebrate it as clean.

Neighbors near the Roscoe complex have been asking for water testing for four years. The turbines leak. The service roads erode into the creeks. The access pads shed gravel and herbicide residue downhill into the playa system. None of this was disclosed in the original permitting, and none of it is being addressed now.

The decommissioning bond the developer posted is a joke. Thirty-five thousand dollars per turbine will not cover the cost of cutting up one blade, let alone hauling 280 of them to a landfill that may or may not accept them. When this project reaches the end of its useful life, Gratiot County will be left with a graveyard of fiberglass and rebar, and the LLC that owns the project will have dissolved years earlier.

Planning Board comment, Town of Hartwick: The applicant's Article 10 filing is conspicuously silent on PFAS leaching from blade coatings, oil and hydraulic fluid spills from gearboxes, and the fate of 600 tonnes of concrete foundation per tower that will remain buried in our aquifer recharge zone long after the project is abandoned. We are being asked to accept a permanent contamination liability in exchange for 25 years of intermittent power.

We are told these are renewable. Renewable in what sense? The turbines are not renewable. The blades are not renewable. The rare earth magnets are not renewable. The concrete pads are not renewable. What is renewable is the subsidy, which gets renewed every few years by a Congress that cannot be bothered to read the balance sheet.

Letter to the editor: I drove past the old Altamont repowering site last month and counted at least a dozen decommissioned blades stacked like carcasses in a gravel lot. Nobody seems to have a plan for them. The companies took their tax credits and left the mess behind, and taxpayers will be picking up the tab for decades. This is not clean energy. It is industrial garbage with a PR budget.

Residents of Osage County have been dealing with oil sheens on stock ponds downhill from the Mustang Run facility for nearly two years. The company denies responsibility. The state agency says it lacks jurisdiction. Meanwhile the cattle will not drink from the east pasture anymore and nobody is answering the phone.

The proposed Buckhorn Ridge wind facility sits directly atop the most heavily used snowmobile corridor in the county, and local clubs have already warned that grooming operations will be impossible once the access roads and turbine pads are cut into the ridgeline. For families who have trailered up here every winter for three generations, this is not a minor inconvenience. It is the end of a recreational tradition that supports dozens of small businesses from the diner in town to the motel on Route 12.

The Wampum River canoe trail, designated a state water trail in 2004, will run directly beneath the collector line crossing proposed in the application. Paddlers will portage around construction staging for at least two summers, and the scenic designation that justified the trail's creation will have to be reviewed once turbines dominate the skyline at every bend.

The saddest part is watching the kids' sailing school look at relocating. They've run out of that pier since the 1960s. The parents' association has been told in no uncertain terms that the construction vessel traffic and the eventual exclusion zones around the turbines make the existing instructional area unsafe for small craft.

The local snowmobile federation, the ATV club, and the horseman's association submitted a joint letter to the county commissioners opposing the project on the grounds that the haul road network and the permanent service roads will fragment the shared-use trail system that all three groups have cooperatively maintained for over two decades.

Cross-country ski groomers told the planning board that the access road grades proposed by the developer will permanently close two of the five loops at the community trail system. Skiers have donated labor and equipment to maintain those trails for 30 years, and they were given no meaningful opportunity to weigh in before the route was finalized.

The town's comments to the Public Service Commission focused on the impact to the municipal beach and the adjacent boat launch. Summer visitors come for the uninterrupted horizon, officials argued, and the loss of that amenity — along with reduced sailing room and the industrialization of what has been a quiet recreational harbor — will hollow out the seasonal economy that the village depends on.

Surfers at the Point have organized against the proposed cable landing, arguing that trenching through the reef will alter wave formation and end a surf break that has drawn competitive surfers to this stretch of coast since the 1970s.

At the zoning hearing, a retired schoolteacher stood up and said what a lot of people were thinking. "I walk the rail-trail every morning. My grandchildren ride it on weekends. If that developer gets his way, we will be walking underneath a row of machines twice the height of anything in this county, and the trail we fought for thirty years to build will never feel the same."

Testimony from the regional golf course superintendents' association pointed out that three of the four courses within five miles of the project will be within the shadow flicker zone during peak afternoon play. Beyond the nuisance to golfers, the association warned, the visual dominance of the turbines over the signature holes will damage the destination-golf reputation the region has cultivated.

I grew up kayaking these waters. My father taught me, and I taught my kids. The idea that we are going to paddle out past a forest of turbines with exclusion buoys and service vessels churning through what used to be quiet coves is heartbreaking, and it is being sold to us as progress.

It is not just the fishermen. Anyone who has ever taken a boat out of Harbor Point knows the shoals are where you go to get away. Put 90 turbines out there and you've turned a weekend refuge into an industrial site, full stop. The developer's recreational use study is a joke — they counted boats on a Wednesday in April.

Opposition to the Rollins Mountain expansion has grown steadily since the Appalachian Trail Conservancy released its viewshed analysis showing that hikers would see turbines for nearly nine miles of the ridge walk. For a trail that draws thousands of thru-hikers and day users each year, the loss of that wilderness experience is not something that can be mitigated with a tree buffer.

Written comments from the regional chapter of Trout Unlimited raised specific concerns about stream crossings along the access road corridor, noting that three of the affected reaches are classified as Class I wild trout waters and support a catch-and-release fishery that contributes significantly to the county's outdoor recreation economy.

Opponents of the Cedar Flats project filed a 120-page brief detailing impacts to the state recreation area, including loss of scenic overlook use, disruption of the established mountain bike trail network, and interference with the night-sky designation that draws astronomy groups from three states. None of these impacts, they argue, were seriously analyzed in the developer's application.

Duck hunters on the flyway are livid. The proposed offshore array sits squarely on the approach corridor that waterfowl have used for as long as anyone has kept records, and the state guides' association has warned that the combination of bird displacement and restricted navigation during hunting season will effectively end commercial guided hunts in the sound.

Members of the Lake Pendleton Sailing Association told the siting board on Tuesday that the turbine array proposed for the shoals will make the annual regatta course unworkable. Wake turbulence, restricted zones around each monopile, and the sheer visual dominance of 700-foot structures will drive racers to other venues. "We've hosted this regatta for 58 years," the commodore said. "It will not survive this project."

We have spent twenty years building this community around outdoor recreation — the mountain biking, the fly fishing, the rock climbing on the south face. Every single one of those activities takes place within sight of the ridgeline the developer now wants to cover in turbines. You cannot separate the recreation economy from the landscape that makes it possible.

Local birders, who have documented migration counts at the bluff for over forty years, warn that the proposed turbines will not only kill raptors but will also end the annual hawk watch that brings enthusiasts from across the region to the overlook each September.

Sportsmen's clubs across the three-county region have come out against the Windy Gap proposal, pointing out that the transmission corridor alone will cut through some of the best upland bird cover in the state. Hunters who have leased those fields for decades say access will be restricted during construction and that the altered landscape will push game populations out entirely.

The county parks commission's written comments to the developer note that the proposed setbacks do not account for the heavily used equestrian trail system that runs along the eastern property line. Horses are known to spook at shadow flicker and low-frequency noise, and the commission warned that the trails — in use since the 1930s — may have to be closed outright if the project is approved as drawn.

Charter captains operating out of the inlet testified that the lease area overlaps with the most productive recreational fishing grounds on this stretch of coast. "You can move a wind farm on paper," one captain said, "but you cannot move the fish. And when the cable trenching tears up the bottom structure, the tog and the sea bass are not coming back on any timeline that matters to my business."

What the company calls "co-use of the ocean" is nothing of the sort. Anybody who has tried to run a sportfishing boat through an active wind lease knows the insurance carriers won't cover you, the Coast Guard recommends you stay clear, and the recreational experience — the reason people pay to come out with us — is destroyed by the industrial sightlines.

Testimony before the Illinois Commerce Commission, Champaign County Farmers for Responsible Siting: The developer's own shadow-flicker modeling shows 34 hours per year of flicker across our soybean fields. At planting and harvest, operators experience documented disorientation in strobing light. This is not a theoretical hazard — it is an occupational injury waiting to happen to farmers who have worked this ground safely for fifty years.

The Kansas Livestock Association passed a resolution at its annual convention opposing further wind development on native rangeland. Ranchers reported that cattle refuse to graze within sight of operating turbines and that calving rates have dropped on leased pastures adjacent to the Flat Ridge II facility. "We've been running cows on this grass since my great-grandfather homesteaded," said Barber County rancher Mike Beam. "The turbines came in and the herd behavior changed overnight."

"Prime ag ground is non-renewable," McLean County Farm Bureau president Rob Hoeft told the zoning board. "We are the third most productive county in the third most productive state in the most productive country in the world. And you want to put 650-foot turbines on Drummer silty clay loam? That's soil that took ten thousand years to form. The turbines will be scrapped in twenty-five years and the land will never farm the same."

The Wisconsin Farm Bureau submitted written testimony against the proposed Sauk Prairie wind project, noting that 14,000 acres of Class I agricultural soils would be locked under easements for decades. "You can't rotate corn and soybeans around a 600-foot turbine," bureau president Dale Kemmeter told the Public Service Commission. "Compaction from crane pads and access roads permanently destroys the topsoil our families spent generations building."

Welsh hill-farmer Dafydd Morgan told BBC Radio Cymru that the Bryn Blaen extension would cross three generations of shepherding tracks and fragment the hefted flock system that sustains upland agriculture. "These sheep know this mountain because their mothers and grandmothers knew it. You run a five-kilometre access road through the middle of that and the heft is broken. You can't just herd them around a windfarm. It's the end of a way of farming that's older than the English language."

Tasmanian Farmers and Graziers Association CEO Nathan Calman said the Robbins Island proposal would industrialise some of the state's most productive fattening country. "We export beef into premium Asian markets on the strength of a clean, green image. Lining the coast with 270-metre turbines undermines the brand our producers have spent three decades building, and it takes grazing country out of production at the same time."

A study commissioned by the Iowa Corn Growers Association found that turbine-induced turbulence measurably alters microclimate conditions in adjacent fields, with surface temperature fluctuations and altered dew formation reducing yields in a 400-meter downwind band. "Farmers near the MidAmerican project in Adair County have been reporting this for years," said ICGA policy director Stu Swanson. "Now we have the data."

Oxford County NDP MPP Ernie Hardeman said prime Class 1 farmland should never have been offered up for industrial wind contracts under the Green Energy Act. "Ontario imports vegetables we used to grow here. Why are we paving our best soils with turbine bases and concrete access roads? Once that ground is out of production, it's out forever."

Submission to the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission from the Liverpool Plains Agricultural Alliance: The Hills of Gold project proposes 70 turbines across some of the most productive dryland cropping country in Australia. Soil surveys identify the site as predominantly black vertosol — the same soil that makes this region the 'breadbasket of the north.' To sacrifice this land for intermittent generation is an act of agricultural vandalism.

Op-ed by Irish Farmers' Association president Francie Gorman, Irish Examiner: The wind industry likes to present itself as a partner to rural Ireland. The reality on the ground is different. Suckler farmers in Leitrim and Donegal are seeing their commonage grazings cut up by haul routes. Tillage farmers in the east are watching prime land taken out of rotation for twenty-five years. And the payments to a handful of lease-holders do nothing to compensate the wider parish for the loss of productive agricultural capacity.

Minnesota Farmers Union policy resolution, adopted at the state convention: "Whereas industrial wind developments increasingly target the state's prime agricultural regions, and whereas the construction of turbine foundations, access roads, and collection systems permanently impairs drainage, soil structure, and field operations, be it resolved that MFU opposes any siting of utility-scale wind generation on soils rated Class I or II without the unanimous written consent of all farming operators within one mile of proposed infrastructure."

Public comment, Knox County Iowa Board of Adversity, from row-crop farmer Janet Veldhuizen: "I farm 1,800 acres my grandfather broke out in 1932. The developer says the turbines will only take two acres out of production per unit. What they don't say is that the access roads, the collection lines, and the substation fence off corners of fields that no longer pay to farm. You lose ten, fifteen acres per turbine once you count the edges. Across forty turbines, that's a half-section of Iowa's best gone."

Dairy farmer Pieter Jansen told the provincial hearing in Friesland that milk production on his 140-cow operation fell by eleven percent in the twelve months after the adjacent windpark was commissioned. "The vet ruled out mastitis, ruled out feed changes. The only variable was the turbines. My neighbors report the same. The province promised a rural energy transition — what we got was the slow ruin of our farms."

Huron County commissioners heard nearly four hours of testimony Tuesday from sugar beet and dry bean growers who said the NextEra proposal would render aerial application impossible across 22,000 contiguous acres. "Our yields depend on timely fungicide passes," said fourth-generation farmer Curt Rapson. "Ground rigs can't cover the acreage in the window we have. If these turbines go up, we're looking at a 15 to 20 percent hit on every bushel — and that's before you count the drainage tile they'll tear out."

The German Bauernverband (Farmers' Association) reports that land rents in Brandenburg have risen 47 percent in five years, driven largely by wind developer speculation on arable parcels. Young farmers attempting to establish operations cannot compete with lease offers backed by the EEG feed-in tariff. "We are pricing the next generation of farmers out of their own heimat," said regional chairman Henrik Wendorff.

Submission from the Federated Farmers of New Zealand to the Environment Canterbury hearing on the Mt Cass windfarm: The proposed site encompasses 620 hectares of established sheep and beef country. Stock handling, mustering by helicopter, and aerial topdressing would all be compromised by the turbine array. The cumulative effect on the operation's viability has not been adequately addressed in the applicant's assessment, and the agricultural productivity loss has been systematically understated.

Op-ed, Drovers: American beef producers are being squeezed from every direction, and now the federal PTC is driving a wind-land-rush across the Sandhills and the Flint Hills. Brokers are offering ranchers four-figure-per-turbine annual payments that sound attractive until you realize your neighbor's lease restricts your ability to burn, to move cattle through easements, or to expand your own operation. Rural communities that have run cattle for 150 years are being pulled apart by a subsidy scheme written in Washington.

At the Saskatchewan Agricultural Hall of Fame luncheon, retiring producer Lorne Scott warned that the province's rush to site wind on cultivated prairie was "a betrayal of the soil." He cited Statistics Canada data showing that 89 percent of the province's installed wind capacity sits on Class 2 or better farmland. "We spent a century learning how to farm these soils sustainably. Now we're burying them under concrete for a twenty-five-year lease."

Letter to the editor, Kildare Nationalist: Farmers in this parish have worked the same drumlin fields for six generations. Now we are told that an 'energy park' of 180m turbines is to be constructed across the best grazing land in the county. Dairy yields drop when cows are stressed by low-frequency noise — any vet will tell you. The silage ground will be cut up by haul roads the width of a motorway. This is the end of farming in Ballitore, plain and simple.

Vermont apple grower Terry Bradshaw testified before the Public Utility Commission that the proposed ridgeline project would eliminate the pollinator corridor connecting his orchard to conserved hardwood forest. "Wild bee populations are already stressed. You put a five-mile string of turbines along that ridge and you've severed the last intact hedgerow system in the valley. My yields depend on native pollinators. I can't just truck in more hives."

Ohio Farmers Union president Joe Logan warned that the setback reductions proposed in HB 197 would allow 200-meter turbines within 600 feet of cultivated fields. "You're going to see shadow flicker across the cab of every combine for half the harvest. You're going to see ice throw onto cornfields in January. And the tile drainage — nobody has a plan for what happens when a turbine foundation severs a century-old tile main."

A Michigan State University extension bulletin, widely circulated among Thumb-region growers, documents reduced pheasant and insect-pollinator counts in fields adjacent to operating wind facilities, with measurable knock-on effects for specialty seed producers. "The ecological simplification around turbine arrays is not benign," the authors write. "For farms that depend on pollination services or integrated pest management, the impacts are real and recurring."

The Scottish Crofting Federation has formally objected to the Strathy South windfarm extension, citing irreversible damage to blanket peat and the displacement of hill-sheep grazing that has underpinned the local economy since the Clearances. "Each turbine base requires the excavation of thousands of cubic metres of peat," said federation chair Yvonne White. "The hydrology of the entire hill is altered. Crofters downslope report their in-bye land waterlogging in seasons it never did before."

At issue in the pending litigation is whether the easement recorded in 1987 for a utility distribution line can now be reinterpreted, 35 years later, to permit the installation of a 230 kV collector line serving a commercial wind facility. The landowners argue this is a fundamental expansion of the burden on their servient estate that was never contemplated, never negotiated, and never compensated — and that allowing it would render rural easements limitless in scope.

The Sámi Reindeer Herders' Association has challenged the Storheia wind development before the Norwegian Supreme Court, arguing that the 151-turbine complex blocks traditional winter grazing migrations and therefore constitutes an unlawful interference with herding rights guaranteed under Article 27 of the ICCPR. The court ruled the licenses invalid, yet the turbines remain in place years later.

Residents of Tiree and Lewis have voiced frustration that crofting tenants, who hold statutory use rights but not freehold title, were largely excluded from lease negotiations conducted between developers and absentee landlords. Entire generations of working crofts may be subject to turbine construction without the actual occupiers having any seat at the table.

Planning objection submitted by M. Okafor: I am the registered proprietor of Lot 14. The applicant's site plan shows an underground cable route and two access tracks traversing my land. No servitude has been granted. No compensation has been offered. No correspondence has been received. I request the application be refused on the ground that it presupposes rights over private property that the applicant does not possess.

Letter to the editor: The wind company's representative told me at my kitchen table that if enough of my neighbors signed, my farm would become a 'holdout parcel' and I'd be stuck surrounded by turbines regardless. That's not a negotiation — that's a threat against my right to decide what happens on land I've paid taxes on for 38 years.

Across the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Zapotec and Ikoots communities report that lease agreements for wind concessions were signed in Spanish with farmers who primarily speak indigenous languages, and that the 30-year terms effectively alienate communal ejido land that residents believed could not be transferred. Several community assemblies have since voted to nullify the contracts, but developers continue operating on the disputed parcels.

The developer's 'good neighbor' payment of $2,000 a year is not compensation for the loss of my right to use the southern 80 acres of my farm however I choose. It is a pittance offered in exchange for surrendering a property right that existed long before anyone discovered it was windy out here.

The developer's representative acknowledged under questioning at the public hearing that the project relies on 'participation agreements' with non-participating neighbors — meaning that in order to site turbines close to property lines, the company secures waivers of noise and setback rights from adjacent owners. Several of those waivers, it emerged, were obtained in exchange for one-time payments of $500 and were signed without legal counsel.

Farmers in the Oaxacan community of Unión Hidalgo say the wind concession contracts, some running 30 years with automatic renewals, were negotiated individually rather than through the communal agrarian assembly as required by law. The result, they argue, is that collectively held ejido land has been effectively privatized into industrial lease parcels without the community ever having voted on it.

County commissioners should understand that when they approve a 60,000-acre wind overlay district, they are not just approving turbines on the 200 farms that signed. They are encumbering every non-participating parcel inside that boundary with noise easements, flicker zones, and construction traffic servitudes that the owners never agreed to and will never be compensated for.

At Tuesday's zoning board meeting, attorney Marlene Cosgrove presented affidavits from seven landowners in the project footprint who said they were told by leasing agents that signing was 'essentially mandatory' because the county had already approved the project. Three of those landowners are now seeking to void their contracts on grounds of misrepresentation and duress.

I don't oppose wind energy on principle. I oppose a legal regime in which a developer, an absentee landlord, and a county board can collectively decide that my family's 160 acres will be ringed by 600-foot structures, and in which my only recourse is to sell at a depressed price to the very company that depressed it. Property is not just a deed. It is the right to say no.

The proposed easement across the Henderson family ranch would give the developer perpetual access to a 40-foot corridor for transmission lines, and we've been told that if we don't sign, they'll simply condemn the land under the state's eminent domain statute. My grandfather homesteaded this property in 1912. No company from out of state should be able to take a ribbon through the middle of it because a utility decided a wind farm three counties over needed to connect to the grid.

Under the revised state siting law, a landowner's refusal to lease can be overridden if a project is designated as being of 'regional energy significance.' In plain English, that means a developer can petition the state commission to run collection lines, access roads, and met towers across your property whether you consent or not. This is the quiet erosion of rural property rights, dressed up in climate language.

Mapuche communities in the Araucanía region have opposed the expansion of wind development onto lands that were restored to them under the Indigenous Law of 1993, arguing that the government's subsequent granting of surface concessions to energy companies unilaterally re-encumbers title that was supposed to be inalienable. The dispute is now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The setback ordinance as currently drafted is a taking. If my neighbor signs a lease and a turbine goes up 1,500 feet from our shared fence, I lose the ability to build a barn, a second home, or even a pole shed within a quarter mile of my own property line — because the developer's noise contour now extends onto MY land. I never signed anything. Why do I lose use of my own acres?

In Kenya's Lake Turkana region, pastoralist groups have pursued a long-running case alleging that 150,000 acres of community land were transferred to the wind consortium without free, prior, and informed consent. A 2021 ruling by the Environment and Land Court found the original land allocation irregular, but the turbines had already been spinning for three years by the time the judgment came down.

Residents of the Dhofar highlands have filed a formal grievance alleging that tribal grazing lands were surveyed and staked for turbine foundations without any consultation with the families who have held customary use rights for generations. The developer maintains that the concession was granted lawfully by the national authority, but locals argue the state had no standing to transfer land it never recognized them as owning in the first place.

When the township passed the wind overlay, it effectively rezoned my property without notifying me, without a hearing specific to my parcel, and without offering any mechanism to opt out. I still pay agricultural-use taxes, but I can no longer build a second residence for my son within the setback buffer of a turbine my neighbor leased. That is a regulatory taking and it will be litigated.

I attended the open house last week and asked the project manager point-blank: if I don't sign, can you still put a turbine on my neighbor's field 900 feet from my bedroom window? He said yes. I asked what recourse I had. He said I could 'engage with the permitting process.' That is not property rights. That is being told you're a spectator to your own dispossession.

Testimony before the Public Service Commission revealed that Invenergy's outreach consultant had flagged, in an internal memo dated March 2022, that "opposition from the Hebron Road corridor is likely to intensify without sustained direct engagement." The memo was not shared with the town board, and no additional meetings were scheduled in that corridor before the application was filed.

The company says it held two open-house sessions, but those were advertised only on a Facebook page nobody in this valley follows, and both were held during working hours on weekdays. When Mrs. Alvarez and a group of neighbours asked for a Saturday meeting in Spanish, they were told the "engagement period" had closed.

Residents along Route 12 say the only notice they received of the blasting schedule for the substation foundation was a flyer tucked under their windshield wipers at the IGA parking lot. Several of them keep horses within a half mile of the site and had no opportunity to arrange alternate boarding before the work began.

Supervisor Klaassen pressed the developer's representative on why the sound monitoring protocol had been finalised before a single public meeting was held in the township. The representative replied that the protocol followed "industry best practice." Klaassen responded: "That's not what I asked. I asked why the people who have to live with it weren't in the room when it was written."

Residents of Clare County told the planning committee Tuesday that they first learned of the 14-turbine Ballynagran proposal through a legal notice in the local paper, weeks after the scoping report had already been submitted. "There was no town hall, no mailer, nothing," said Fiona Hegarty, who farms within 900 metres of the proposed site. "We had to request the documents through a solicitor. That is not consultation, that is a tick-box exercise designed to run out the clock on objections."

The Standing Rock of the North, some are calling it. Tribal elders say they were notified of the transmission corridor associated with the wind project only after easements had already been signed with adjacent ranchers. "They came to us last," said council member Dale Red Feather. "They came to us when the route was fixed and the only thing left to discuss was the colour of the access gates."

A freedom-of-information request filed by Concerned Citizens of Lapeer County revealed that the developer had met privately with the township supervisor on at least eleven occasions between October and June, while the first public information session was not held until July — by which point the site plan had already been substantially finalised.

"Meaningful consultation," under the Aarhus Convention, requires that the public be given the opportunity to participate when all options are still open and before decisions have effectively been made. What we have seen in the Killala Bay application is the precise opposite: a preferred bidder selected, a grid connection secured, and a lease executed — all before the first public information session was advertised.

Town hall attendance was limited to those who had pre-registered online 72 hours in advance. Several elderly residents without internet access were turned away at the door. The developer's facilitator described the event as "well attended by stakeholders who had taken the time to prepare."

From the public comment period transcript, p. 142: "I drove two hours to be here tonight. I was given three minutes. The developer has had eighteen months of closed-door meetings with your staff. Tell me again how this process is balanced."

The Vermont Public Service Board received more than 1,400 individual letters objecting to the Lowell Mountain project during the final comment window. In its order approving the Certificate of Public Good, the Board devoted three paragraphs to the objections — most of that summarising, not engaging, the concerns raised. For the residents who had spent months preparing those submissions, the message was unmistakable.

Parents at the Glenbrook Primary School gathered outside the council chambers last night, holding signs that read "We Are The Neighbours You Forgot." The school sits 640 metres from turbine T-07 of the approved Mount Fraser array, yet the school board confirmed it was never formally consulted during the environmental assessment phase.

"They held the meeting in the next town over," said Mr. Ballinger, whose farm abuts two of the proposed turbine locations. "Forty-five minutes away, at seven o'clock on a Wednesday in February. If you didn't drive, or you were on evening shift at the hospital, or you had kids to put to bed, you were not part of that so-called community conversation."

"They called it a workshop," Mrs. Okonkwo told the community radio station. "But when I raised my hand to ask about the compensation formula, the facilitator said that was not on the agenda for that evening and would be addressed at a later session. That later session never happened."

A coalition of twelve homeowners' associations across Ottawa and Renfrew Counties issued a joint statement this week accusing the Independent Electricity System Operator and project proponents of "systematic exclusion" of affected residents from siting decisions. The statement notes that the so-called Municipal Support Resolution process gives host townships a vote but leaves neighbouring municipalities — often within the 3-kilometre impact zone — with no formal standing at all.

The grievance is not that we lost the argument. The grievance is that we were never admitted to it. Meetings were scheduled and cancelled, documents were released in redacted form at the end of the statutory period, and our technical consultant's questions on infrasound modelling were referred to an email address that auto-replied for six weeks. This is what the industry now calls "engagement."

In submissions to the Environment and Communications References Committee, the Waubra Foundation and several individual residents argued that AGL's community engagement for the Hallett extension amounted to little more than a mailing list and a hotline that rang through to a call centre in Adelaide. Concerns raised about low-frequency noise and shadow flicker were, they said, "logged and ignored."

The Nation's traditional council passed a resolution Monday declaring that the free, prior and informed consent standard had not been met for the proposed 320 MW development on ceded territory. The developer disputes this, pointing to a signed MOU with the elected band council, but traditional leadership argues that the MOU was negotiated in camera and that the broader membership was never given access to the draft terms.

Letter to the Editor: I have attended every single one of the so-called "community liaison" meetings held by Northgate Renewables over the past eighteen months. At each one we were handed glossy brochures, shown a looping video, and told our questions would be "taken back to the technical team." Not one substantive answer has ever come back. The developer treats consultation as a performance, not a conversation, and the county planners appear content to play along.

In her closing statement to the regional planning tribunal, counsel for the Friends of the Moor argued that the applicant had treated the statutory consultation as "an obstacle to be managed" rather than a mechanism for genuine dialogue. She cited seven specific concerns raised during scoping — on peat hydrology, raptor flight paths, and cumulative visual impact — none of which, she said, received a substantive response in the final environmental statement.

Mr. Haldorsen, a retired fisheries biologist who submitted a 40-page technical objection, told the inquiry that he received a single-paragraph acknowledgement from the developer stating his concerns had been "noted and considered." No response addressed any of the substantive points. "That is not consideration," he said. "That is filing."

Testimony submitted to the New York State Public Service Commission by the Long Island Commercial Fishing Association notes that survey vessels associated with Sunrise Wind and Empire Wind have displaced trawlers from historically productive areas for more than 18 months, with no meaningful mitigation. The association argues that cumulative effects across multiple lease areas have not been adequately studied, and that small, family-owned operations will be forced out of business long before a single turbine generates power.

The Point Judith Fishermen's Cooperative warned state officials Tuesday that the proposed 62-turbine array south of Block Island would cut directly through squid and fluke grounds that have sustained three generations of trawlers. "If you put monopiles in the middle of our tow lanes, you don't just inconvenience us — you end us," said cooperative president Marco Alvarez. The group is demanding that BOEM redo its economic impact assessment, which they say understated annual landings by more than 40 percent.

Op-ed, Cape May County Herald: The wind companies keep telling us that fishing and offshore wind can coexist. Ask a longliner working the Hudson Canyon whether he can safely set gear among monopiles in a fog. Ask a scalloper whether a dragger's cables play nice with buried transmission lines. The answer, in both cases, is a word this newspaper cannot print.

Comments filed by the Garden State Seafood Association with the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities warned that the economic model used to justify Atlantic Shores Phase 1 failed to account for displaced fishing effort, increased steaming time to alternative grounds, and the loss of vessel insurance coverage for boats operating inside turbine arrays. The association characterized the state's analysis as "a fiction written to support a predetermined conclusion."

Scottish creel fishermen operating out of Fraserburgh say the Moray West development has already forced them out of traditional grounds they have worked since the 1970s. Cables laid across the seabed make setting pots impossible in large swaths of what used to be productive lobster and prawn territory, and compensation offers from the developer have been described by the Scottish Creel Fishermen's Federation as "insulting and wholly inadequate."

A joint statement from fishing associations in Normandy and Brittany decried the Saint-Brieuc and Fécamp wind projects as an "expropriation of the sea." Scallop dredgers in particular say that exclusion zones imposed during both construction and operation have eliminated access to beds representing, in some cases, more than half of a vessel's annual revenue.

letter to the editor: my husband has fished out of barnegat light for 38 years. he is watching his livelihood disappear under a forest of steel that nobody who lives here asked for. the fluke are moving, the scallop beds are being surveyed by boats that don't know one end of a dredge from the other, and our governor keeps telling us this is progress. progress for whom?

Every time a pile driver rings out across these waters, it rings down the price of tomorrow's catch. The mackerel scatter. The haddock move. The bluefin chase bait that is no longer where it used to be. And the men who go out at three in the morning to feed their families come home to tell their wives that maybe, next year, the kid won't be going to college after all.

Vietnamese-American fishermen working out of Biloxi have raised concerns about proposed wind development in the Gulf of Mexico, noting that language barriers and short public comment windows have effectively excluded them from the federal leasing process. Community advocates say BOEM's outreach amounted to little more than a PDF on a government website, while the livelihoods of hundreds of small-boat shrimpers hang in the balance.

When the developers came to our village council meeting, they brought a slideshow and a catered lunch. What they did not bring was a single answer to the question every fisherman in the room was asking: where are we supposed to go when you put two hundred turbines on top of the grounds we have fished for forty years? They smiled, thanked us for our input, and left. Three weeks later, the lease was approved.

The Hokkaido Federation of Fisheries Cooperative Associations has formally objected to three proposed floating wind projects in the Sea of Japan, noting that pile-driving noise during construction is projected to overlap with the peak spawning period for Pacific herring. Cooperative leaders have accused METI of downplaying fisheries impacts in its environmental reviews in order to meet national renewable energy targets.

Dr. Meghan Lapp of Seafreeze Ltd. testified that federal agencies have consistently failed to model cumulative socioeconomic impacts on the commercial fishing sector, instead reviewing each lease area in isolation. "When you add it all up — Vineyard Wind, Revolution, South Fork, Sunrise, Empire, Beacon, Atlantic Shores — you are looking at the industrialization of the entire mid-Atlantic and Northeast continental shelf, and the end of a working waterfront that feeds this country."

Korean cuttlefish fishermen blockaded the harbor at Yeonggwang last month in protest of an 8.2 GW offshore wind complex planned off the southwest coast. Boat owners say that the developer, a consortium including foreign majority shareholders, has refused to release the full benthic survey data and has offered lump-sum payments that amount to less than two years of average earnings.

The Taiwanese fishing communities around Changhua have repeatedly petitioned the Ministry of Economic Affairs over the Greater Changhua offshore wind projects. Local fishermen report sharp declines in catches of finless porpoise bycatch — long used as an indicator species — and say pile-driving during construction coincided with the worst squid season in living memory. Compensation schemes, they argue, benefit a small number of association leaders while ordinary boat owners receive nothing.

Danish fishermen once held up as proof that offshore wind and fishing could coexist have been telling a different story in recent years. Members of the Danish Fishermen's Producer Organisation report being pushed out of Horns Rev and Anholt, with promised co-use arrangements never materializing. "They used us for the photos," one skipper told a reporter from Fiskeri Tidende. "Now they don't return our calls."

testimony before the maine legislature's energy committee: "the gulf of maine is not an empty parking lot waiting to be filled with turbines. it is a working ecosystem, and lobstermen are part of that ecosystem. research leases granted without lobstering community consent are a breach of the social contract that has governed these waters for over a century."

the groundfishermen of gloucester have survived the cod collapse, the catch share wars, and every bureaucratic indignity washington could throw at them. now they are being told, without so much as a phone call, that their grounds will be leased to a danish multinational for the next thirty-five years. tell me again who the environmentalists are working for.

During the public hearing in New Bedford, Captain Jim Kendall reminded the panel that the port is the highest-grossing commercial fishing port in the nation and that Vineyard Wind's turbine layout was set without meaningful input from the men and women who actually work those waters. "They drew lines on a map," he said. "We drew our lives on that map decades ago."

A report commissioned by the Responsible Offshore Development Alliance concluded that proposed wind lease areas in the New York Bight overlap with more than 60 percent of the surfclam fishery's active grounds. Industry representatives say the loss of access, combined with reduced vessel transit speeds through turbine arrays for safety reasons, could collapse a fishery that supplies the bulk of domestic clam chowder production.

Speaker at Montauk town hall: "My grandfather fished these waters. My father fished these waters. I fish these waters. And now I'm being told by people in Albany who have never pulled a net in their lives that my grandson will not. That is not a clean energy transition — that is a taking, plain and simple, and somebody ought to be held accountable."

the department of the interior has effectively declared that commercial fishing families are an acceptable casualty of the energy transition. nowhere in the record of decision for the new england wind project will you find a credible accounting of the lost catches, the ruined gear, the family boats sold at auction, or the seventh-generation captains forced into retirement. you will, however, find glossy renderings of turbines against a sunset.

What the glossy developer brochures never mention is that every mile of export cable trenched into the seabed is a mile of bottom that won't be fished again for years, if ever. The scallopers know it. The draggers know it. The only people who don't seem to know it are the regulators rubber-stamping construction and operations plans from offices four hundred miles inland.

Realtors in our county are already reporting it. Two closings fell apart last month once buyers did a title search and noticed the meteorological towers going up three parcels over. You can disclose all you want, but when a family drives out and sees that 600-foot silhouette looming over the pasture, they keep driving. The appraiser I spoke with, who has 30 years in the business, said homes within a mile of an operating project in the neighboring township have lost roughly 18 to 22 percent of their pre-announcement value, and that's being generous.

Selectman Briggs noted that the town's own consultant, in a report commissioned independently of the developer, concluded that residential properties within the viewshed of the proposed turbines could reasonably be expected to experience value reductions of 5 to 12 percent, with properties on ridgelines or within 1 mile of the nearest turbine facing the higher end of that range. The board voted 4-1 to recommend denial of the special permit.

During public comment, Reverend Carla Mendenhall of First Methodist read a letter on behalf of three elderly parishioners who had asked to remain anonymous. Each had attempted to sell their homes in the past year and each had received offers significantly below assessed value, with buyers' agents specifically citing the turbine project. "These are women on fixed incomes," Reverend Mendenhall told the board. "They cannot afford to lose twenty or thirty thousand dollars because this company wants to build where it shouldn't."

The Berkeley Lab reports frequently cited by the industry to dismiss property value concerns rely on sales data dominated by projects with much smaller turbines — typically under 100 meters in total height — sited at setbacks that would be considered generous by current standards. Extrapolating those findings to contemporary 200-meter machines sited at 1,500 feet from residences is not science. It is marketing.

Board of Assessment Appeals, Case No. 2023-114: The petitioners, owners of a 4.3-acre parcel improved with a single-family residence, seek a reduction in assessed value on the grounds that construction of the Blackstone Wind facility, completed in November 2022, has materially impaired the marketability and fair market value of the subject property. Petitioners submitted three independent appraisals, each indicating a post-construction value reduction of between 16 and 22 percent attributable to proximity, visibility, and acoustic impact of the facility. The Board finds the evidence persuasive and grants the requested reduction.

You want to know why the opposition to this project is so fierce? Walk down any road within two miles of the fence line and look at the for-sale signs that have been up for a year. Look at the price reductions. Talk to the young couple who were ready to buy the old Henderson place until their loan officer told them the bank was nervous about the collateral. This isn't nimbyism. It's people watching their life savings evaporate because somebody in Houston drew a red circle on a map.

We bought this place in 2009. It was our retirement. Everything we had went into the down payment and the addition we put on the back. Now Apex tells us the nearest turbine will be 1,450 feet from our bedroom window and the township attorney says that's perfectly legal under the new ordinance. My wife called three appraisers. Two wouldn't even take the job once they heard the address. The third told us, off the record, to expect a 30 percent hit and to not bother listing until the project is either built or killed.

The developer's glossy brochure promised "no measurable impact" on surrounding property values. Eighteen months after commissioning, the county assessor reduced the taxable value of 43 non-participating parcels within the project footprint, citing market evidence of diminished sale prices and extended days-on-market. When we requested the developer revise its impact study accordingly, the response was that the assessor's reductions were "unrelated to the project." The evidence on the ground says otherwise.

Residents of the proposed Glenford Ridge project area packed the township hall Tuesday to voice concerns ranging from shadow flicker and low-frequency noise to the economic toll on home values. Longtime resident Marjorie Kowalski told trustees she had refinanced last spring at an appraised value of $287,000. "If this goes in," she said, "I'll be underwater the day they pour the first foundation. Nobody from the company will even return my calls about it."

The appraisal industry has a term for what happens to residential property within sight and earshot of an industrial wind facility: encumbrance. It's the same word we use for easements, flood zones, and nearby rail lines. Buyers discount for it. Lenders account for it. Insurance actuaries price it. The only people who seem not to recognize it are the planning boards issuing the permits and the consultants the developers pay to tell them it isn't happening.

Letter to the editor: My neighbor's grandson is trying to sell the family farmhouse after she passed. It's been listed eleven months. Three different agents. Before the turbine company started buying up leases, that place would've been under contract in a weekend. Now? Nothing. The only offer they got came from the wind developer itself, at about sixty cents on the dollar. Tell me again how this project is good for the community.

I sit on the board of our small rural bank and I can tell you what nobody in Madison wants to hear: we are already adjusting our lending criteria for parcels within the proposed Red Oak project boundary. Not because we oppose wind, but because our regulators demand we assess collateral risk honestly. If a 15-year mortgage is underwritten on a house that may lose a fifth of its market value the moment steel goes up, that's a problem for the borrower and for us.

Representative Hollings asked the applicant's witness whether his firm had conducted a paired-sales analysis of properties within the proposed footprint. The witness conceded they had not. Representative Hollings then asked whether the firm had reviewed the 2016 Clarkson University study documenting value losses of 7 to 15 percent for homes within one mile of turbines in northern New York. The witness replied that he was "not familiar with that particular paper." The hearing was recessed shortly thereafter.

A recent working paper from researchers at the London School of Economics, drawing on more than a million UK property transactions, found statistically significant price reductions for homes with a visible wind installation within 2 km, with effects persisting for more than a decade after construction. The authors estimate aggregate losses in the billions of pounds, a figure conspicuously absent from developers' cost-benefit submissions to local planning authorities.

My home is my retirement account. I don't have a pension from the state and I don't have a 401(k) worth talking about. When I sell this house in fifteen years, that's what my wife and I will live on. So when the county board tells me they've approved a 600-foot turbine 1,800 feet from my property line, and that studies they paid for say it won't affect my value, and that my only option is to take the developer's "good neighbor payment" of $2,400 a year and sign away my right to complain, I want them to understand that they are gambling with money that isn't theirs.

Anyone who has tried to sell a home within sight of an operating wind facility knows what the academic literature is only now catching up to. Buyers bring it up unprompted. They ask about noise at night. They ask about the red lights. They ask if the turbines will get taller when the lease is renewed. And then they offer less, or they don't offer at all. It is not a theoretical effect. It is visible in every MLS printout in every county where these things have been built.

Mr. Chairman, I'd like to enter into the record the Lansink study and the more recent work out of the London School of Economics, both of which document measurable property value declines within two kilometers of industrial wind installations. The applicant's consultant dismissed these as outliers, but I note he did not produce a single peer-reviewed paper demonstrating neutral impact. If the board grants this special use permit without any provision for property value guarantees to non-participating landowners, you will be transferring wealth from ordinary homeowners to an out-of-state developer by administrative fiat.

The Ontario Superior Court ruling in Wiggins v. WPD Canada, while ultimately decided on procedural grounds, is notable for the trial judge's observation that evidence of post-construction diminution in residential property values was "substantial and largely uncontroverted." Local boards in Ontario and elsewhere continue to approve projects on the strength of developer-commissioned studies that do not engage seriously with this body of evidence.

The planning inspector's report acknowledges, at paragraph 7.42, that "some diminution in residential amenity and associated property value is probable for a limited number of receptors," before concluding that this harm is outweighed by the public benefit of renewable generation. I would submit to the committee that the inspector has no authority to conduct such a balancing act on behalf of individual homeowners whose single largest asset is being diminished to serve a national target.

The production tax credit doesn't just distort the electricity market. It distorts the land market. Developers can afford to outbid every other use for rural acreage because the federal subsidy guarantees their return regardless of whether the project makes economic sense on its own merits. The result is that non-participating neighbors — who receive none of the lease income but absorb all of the visual, acoustic, and property-value costs — are effectively subsidizing the scheme twice: once as taxpayers, and again as homeowners.

Let's be honest about what a host community agreement really is. It's hush money for the township so they'll sign off while every non-leasing neighbor gets stuck absorbing the losses. The leaseholder gets his $12,000 per turbine per year. The township gets its PILOT payment. And the guy across the road, who refused to sign, watches his biggest asset lose a quarter of its value with no recourse whatsoever. That's not economic development. That's a taking without compensation.

From the Ashford Town Council minutes — 'Councilwoman Briggs asked the developer's representative what specific reduction in atmospheric carbon the project would achieve. The representative stated she did not have that figure available. Councilwoman Briggs observed that this was, in her view, the only question that mattered.'

The central rhetorical trick of the wind industry is to equate installed capacity with climate progress. But capacity is not emissions reduction, and emissions reduction in the United States is not the same as measurable mitigation of a global phenomenon. At each step of that chain, the numbers get smaller. By the end, the climate rationale is nearly invisible.

Blog post, Energy Realities Project: 'It is an article of faith in climate policy circles that building more wind capacity is synonymous with addressing climate change. But faith is not analysis. When you actually run the numbers on marginal abatement — accounting for intermittency, curtailment, and the lifecycle of the machines themselves — the climate return on wind investment ranges from modest to invisible.'

I used to believe wind was part of the solution. Then I read the IPCC's own working-group tables and realized that the emissions pathway models do not actually depend on wind capacity in any load-bearing way. We are being sold a climate rationale that the underlying science does not require and does not support.

The wind lobby keeps telling us these projects are 'critical for meeting our climate goals.' Critical how, exactly? Nobody on the commission could answer when Councilman Reyes asked for a quantified emissions reduction figure tied to the Valley Ridge proposal. The silence was instructive.

Comments submitted to the Public Utilities Commission by Concerned Ratepayers of the Midwest: 'The Commission should require, as a condition of approval, a quantified and peer-reviewable estimate of the project's contribution to global temperature mitigation. Without such a figure, the climate benefits cited throughout the application are merely rhetorical.'

Op-ed, Rural Voice Weekly — Proponents of the Cedar Creek project insist the 42 turbines are 'essential to fighting climate change.' Essential to whom? A back-of-envelope calculation using EIA emissions factors shows the project, over its full operational life, offsets roughly 0.00008 percent of annual global emissions. That is not fighting climate change. That is climate theater.

Written testimony of Dr. Marsha Keller to the House Energy Subcommittee: 'The premise underlying the 45-gigawatt offshore target — that it will meaningfully alter atmospheric CO2 concentrations — has never been empirically demonstrated. The agency's own modeling, when one bothers to read the appendix, concedes the climate signal is below the threshold of detectability.'

A Harvard atmospheric scientist — not a skeptic, a full-throated climate hawk — told a symposium last month that the community needs to stop overselling wind. 'If we pretend these projects solve the problem,' she said, 'we won't build the things that actually do.' Her warning has been almost entirely ignored by the industry.

Even if every proposed turbine in the Great Plains were built tomorrow, the resulting temperature impact by century's end would be a rounding error. The Bjorn Lomborg calculation has been run a dozen ways and always lands in the same ballpark: hundredths of a degree. That is not a climate solution. That is a very expensive gesture.

There is something almost Orwellian about how the phrase 'climate solution' gets slapped on any wind proposal regardless of whether it delivers measurable climate benefits. The label has become a permission slip. Strip it away and demand evidence, and the whole case shrinks to something very small.

An industry-funded white paper released this week claims the Northeast wind corridor will 'play a critical role in meeting climate goals.' Critical role, by their own figures, means about one-tenth of one percent of the reduction the IPCC says would be needed to hold warming below 1.5 degrees. If that is critical, the word has lost all meaning.

Honestly, the whole 'climate emergency requires wind turbines' framing falls apart the moment you look at what the turbines are projected to accomplish. The numbers are so small that the justification collapses into pure symbolism. And symbolism is a very poor reason to industrialize a ridgeline.

Testimony from the Maine Lobstermen's Association hearing: 'We have been told repeatedly that sacrificing traditional fishing grounds is necessary to save the climate. We asked the developers, in writing, three separate times, for the emissions math. We never received it. I suspect we never will, because the math does not support the claim.'

letter to the editor — it amazes me that the same officials who lecture us about 'following the science' cannot produce a single peer-reviewed paper showing that the proposed brookfield project will lower global temperatures by any measurable amount. they cannot, because no such paper exists. the climate justification is assumed, not proven.

The dirty secret of the offshore push is that even the agencies promoting it do not project meaningful climate outcomes. Read the supplementary environmental impact statement — the GHG reductions are presented as 'anticipated' and 'directional,' never as quantified contributions to temperature targets. That is lawyer language for 'we don't actually know.'

In the Senate hearing last Thursday, Senator Ackerman pressed the witness for a number — any number — showing how the proposed offshore lease would affect global temperatures. The witness pivoted to capacity figures, then to jobs, then to 'leadership.' She never produced the number. There is a reason for that.

Guest column — my objection to the Highland Ridge farm is not that I reject climate science. I accept it. My objection is that this project, by its own developer's modeling, will not measurably change the trajectory of warming. We are being asked to accept real, local, permanent harms in exchange for a climate benefit that exists mainly in press releases.

Rep. Thornton, during floor debate: 'My colleagues across the aisle would have you believe that voting against this wind package is voting against the planet. I would submit to the body that voting for it does virtually nothing for the planet either. The climate benefits are asserted, not substantiated, and the costs are all too real.'

Dr. Patel's analysis, published in the Journal of Policy Economics last spring, concluded that the 1.2 trillion dollars slated for global offshore wind expansion through 2040 would, under optimistic assumptions, reduce end-of-century warming by approximately 0.04 degrees Celsius. The paper was peer-reviewed. The industry response has been to ignore it.

From the Rotterdam conference proceedings: several presenters noted that despite two decades of aggressive wind rollout across the North Sea basin, the contribution to global temperature trajectories has been 'statistically unremarkable' — their words, not mine. The policy continues on momentum, not evidence.

Audible turbine noise is only part of the problem. Residents living near the Stonebrook facility also describe a sensation of "pressure" in the ears and chest, particularly at night, which acoustic engineers attribute to low-frequency pulsations below the threshold of conscious hearing. These pulsations are not captured by the A-weighted decibel scale the state uses for compliance monitoring, meaning the facility can be fully compliant on paper while making residents physically ill in practice.

The applicant claims the project will comply with the state's 45 dBA nighttime limit, but that limit was written for steady-state industrial noise and does not account for the amplitude modulation that characterizes modern utility-scale turbines. What residents describe as a "whoomp-whoomp" is exactly the sort of pulsing sound that penetrates walls, wakes sleepers, and cannot be masked by a fan or white-noise machine. Until the Board requires a condition of approval that specifically addresses amplitude modulation and infrasound at property lines, this permit should not issue.

Residents along the ridge in Somerset County filed a complaint with the township last week, stating that the low-frequency thrum from the 18 newly commissioned turbines has become intolerable after dark. "I haven't slept more than four hours a night since they started spinning," said Marlene Whitaker, whose farmhouse sits roughly 1,400 feet from the nearest tower. "It's a deep pulsing that you feel in your chest. My husband has developed migraines he never had before." Several neighbors reported similar symptoms, including tinnitus and dizziness, and are now asking the county health department to commission an independent acoustic study.

Carla Menendez told the county health board that her nine-year-old son, diagnosed with ADHD, has experienced a dramatic worsening of symptoms since the Hollow Creek turbines came online half a mile from their home. His pediatrician has linked the regression directly to sleep deprivation caused by nighttime noise. "He used to sleep. He doesn't anymore. And I have a letter from his doctor that says why," she told the board, holding the letter aloft.

My neighbor Gloria is 76. She raised four children in her house. She buried her husband in the cemetery up the road. Last month she put her home on the market because the wind turbines two fields over have made it impossible for her to sleep. She is leaving the only place she has ever called home because a company from out of state decided her peace was worth less than their profit margin. If you think noise is a minor issue, you have not met Gloria.

The study, published last month in the Journal of Environmental Health Research, followed 412 residents living within 2 kilometers of operating wind facilities across three counties over a 30-month period. Researchers found statistically significant increases in self-reported sleep disturbance, annoyance, and stress-related symptoms compared with a demographically matched control group more than 10 kilometers from any turbine. The authors concluded that setback distances currently in use across most of the Midwest "appear insufficient to protect residents from chronic noise-related health impacts."

Selectman Peter Caldwell read from a letter submitted by a couple who moved away from their home of 31 years after the turbines went up. "We did not want to leave. We had no plans to leave. But after eighteen months of the noise, my wife's blood pressure was uncontrollable and our doctor told us plainly that we had to get out. We sold at a loss. The wind company took our home from us as surely as if they had come in and pushed us out."

Dr. Hastings, an otolaryngologist who has examined more than sixty residents living within a mile of the Black Oak Wind Project, told the commission that he has documented a consistent pattern of sleep disturbance, chronic headaches, and vertigo in his patients since the turbines came online in 2021. "I am not an anti-wind activist," he said. "I am a doctor reporting what I see in my exam room. These symptoms track with proximity to the turbines and resolve when patients stay elsewhere for a week or more. That is a meaningful clinical signal."

At last night's village meeting, 47 of the 52 residents who spoke identified turbine noise as the reason for their opposition to the proposed expansion. Several brought audio recordings made from their bedrooms. One recording, played over the meeting room speakers, produced audible gasps from attendees who had not previously lived near a wind facility. "That is what we hear every night," said the resident who made the recording. "That is why we cannot support this project going forward."

Town officials in Prentiss have acknowledged that the noise complaints received since the Meadowlark facility began operation "exceed in both number and severity" anything anticipated during the permitting process. The board has now hired an independent acoustician to conduct continuous monitoring at six receptor locations, with results expected in the spring. Residents, meanwhile, continue to report sleep loss, stress, and what one called "the feeling that your own home is no longer a refuge."

I am writing on behalf of the 34 families who signed the attached petition. Every one of us lives within one mile of the Prairie Edge wind facility. Every one of us has documented, in writing, sleep disruption, headaches, or ringing in the ears since the turbines were energized in October. This is not a coincidence. This is not imagination. This is a public health problem that the county commission has an obligation to investigate.

The Clare County Zoning Board of Appeals heard nearly four hours of testimony Tuesday night, with the overwhelming majority of speakers citing turbine noise as their primary concern. Several pointed to peer-reviewed studies linking chronic exposure to wind turbine noise with elevated cortisol, hypertension, and what researchers have termed "wind turbine syndrome." A retired nurse held up a sound meter reading she had taken from her back porch: 52 decibels at 11:47 p.m., well above the county's stated nighttime standard.

To the Editor: I moved to Huron County for the quiet. That is gone now. The turbines behind my property line run twenty-four hours a day, and on south-wind nights the noise is loud enough that I can hear it with the windows closed and a box fan running. My grandchildren will not sleep over anymore. The developer told us before construction that we wouldn't hear a thing. They lied, plain and simple, and now we are the ones paying for it with our health.

The Town of Greenvale's noise complaints log, obtained through a public records request, shows 217 separate complaints filed against the Silver Ridge Wind Project between January and August of this year alone. Complaints reference "jet engine" sounds, "thumping that shakes the windows," and one resident described being unable to have a normal conversation in her own backyard. Despite this, the project operator has faced no enforcement action, and the state PSC has yet to respond to the town's formal request for review.

Residents of the small fishing village of Killaney say the six-turbine array commissioned last spring on the headland has transformed their community. "You can hear them over the sound of the sea," said one longtime resident. "My mother, who is 82, has had to move in with my sister in town because the noise was keeping her awake. We lived here all our lives in the quiet, and now they've brought the factory to us."

Opponents of the proposed 48-turbine Cedar Hollow project say the developer's own sound modeling, buried in appendix F of the permit application, predicts exceedances of 40 dBA at 14 nearby residences under certain atmospheric conditions. "They know," said project opponent Lana Kirkwood. "They have put it in writing and they are asking the board to approve it anyway. If the board approves this knowing what is in that appendix, they are knowingly approving harm to their own constituents."

The trouble with the developer's assurances is that they are always future-tense. Before construction: "You won't hear a thing." During construction: "Wait until operations stabilize." After commissioning: "The sound levels are within regulatory limits." Meanwhile the people who have to live underneath these machines are documenting, in diaries and sound recordings and doctor's visits, exactly what the developer promised would never happen.

"Come spend a night at my house," Mr. Donoghue told the planning board members. "Any night you want. I'll make up the guest room. And when you lie there at two in the morning listening to it, you tell me this is something you would approve to go up next to your own family's home." The room was silent. No board member took him up on the offer.

What the developer's noise consultant will not tell you is that their model averages sound over a one-hour period. A turbine that is quiet for fifty-five minutes and thunderous for five will comply with the averaged standard while making life unbearable for the family next door. The ordinance needs to be written in terms of maximum instantaneous levels, L-max, not L-eq, or we are setting our neighbors up for exactly the health complaints we have seen from every other county that went down this road.

A growing body of acoustic research suggests that infrasound and low-frequency noise from wind turbines, though often inaudible, can produce physiological effects including sleep fragmentation and cardiovascular stress. The World Health Organization's 2018 environmental noise guidelines recommended wind turbine noise levels below 45 dB Lden, but explicitly noted that the evidence base for this recommendation was of "low quality" and called for further research. In the meantime, rural residents are serving as the unconsenting subjects of that research.

The Appeals Tribunal found that the 550-meter setback applied by the province is "not supported by the acoustic evidence" and that testimony from affected residents "established, on the balance of probabilities, a causal relationship between operation of the turbines and the sleep disturbance, tinnitus, and chronic headaches reported by witnesses." The tribunal declined to revoke the permit but ordered nighttime curtailment during south-westerly wind conditions.

wind energy 🙄 sure. whatever they say. we all know how this ends
If you support these wind projects you haven't been paying attention. Simple as that. Do your homework and get back to me.

Another wind farm proposal, another round of nonsense. When will it end? Honestly at this point I've stopped being surprised by anything these people try to push through.
Look, I'm not an engineer and I'm not a scientist, but I know a bad deal when I see one. This wind project is a bad deal. End of story.

Public comment, Planning & Zoning Board, 3/14: My name is Robert Steiner, I farm on County Road 12, and I am here tonight to say this project is wrong. I've said so before and I'll keep saying so. Thank you.
From a concerned grandmother in Tipton County: What kind of world are we leaving these kids? I look at those turbines and I just feel sad. I can't explain it any better than that.
Dear Editor — Re: your November 14 editorial endorsing the county's renewable energy plan. I could not disagree more strongly. Shame on this paper.
Testimony of Margaret Hollis, Township Resident: I've said my piece at every one of these hearings going back three years now. I'll say it again. No. Just no.
Another day, another wind farm announcement. Yawn. Wake me up when someone in charge finally figures out this isn't the miracle they keep claiming.
Saw the new turbines going up along Route 9 this weekend. Absolutely sickening. I don't have the words.
You'd have to be living under a rock to still believe the hype around wind power. Come on. We're all adults here.
honestly the whole wind thing is a joke at this point and anyone with two eyes can see it

Did anyone else catch the piece in last Sunday's paper cheerleading for offshore wind? Unreal. The bias is off the charts. At some point you have to wonder who's writing these things.
Commenter @PrairieDad74: Another day, another wind project announcement. Another day of pretending this is going somehow work out fine. Sure. Whatever you say, guys.

Comment, Yorkshire Post online: The whole business is a joke. Honestly. A complete and utter joke. And yet on it goes, year after year, with nobody in Westminster willing to say what everyone in the dales already knows.

Letter to editor, Carbon County Gazette: As a retired schoolteacher and lifelong resident, I feel compelled to write regarding the Buffalo Creek wind proposal. Something about this whole enterprise does not pass the smell test and I trust my neighbors feel the same.

Submitted comment to BOEM docket, lightly edited: I oppose this lease sale. I oppose the next one too. I oppose the entire direction this agency has chosen to go. Respectfully, Capt. R. Donnelly (ret.), Point Judith, RI.
