You know what, I'm done arguing about it. People are going to believe what they want to believe about wind power. I just hope when the bill comes due they remember who was waving the pom-poms.

Letter, Orkney Today: Sir — I have read the latest consultation document from the developers with interest and considerable dismay. I shall be registering my objection formally and I would encourage my fellow islanders to do likewise. Yours, M. Flett, Stromness.

Reply on Nextdoor, Fairview subdivision: Anyone else getting those glossy mailers from Vesper Energy? Straight into the recycling. Don't be fooled — we've seen this movie before and it never ends well for people like us.

Facebook post (public, 847 reactions): They're coming for our ridgeline next. I heard it straight from a guy who works at the county office. If you think this isn't going to happen here you haven't been paying attention. Wake up people.

Final remarks, public hearing transcript, Huron County, MI: Mr. Chairman, with respect, I've sat through six of these hearings now and I'll sit through six more if that's what it takes. This is not over. Not by a long shot. Thank you.

Dr. Marion Feld, an ornithologist formerly with the state wildlife agency, told the legislative energy committee that the incidental take permitting scheme for wind projects has effectively become a rubber stamp. "In the fourteen years I worked on these applications, I can count on one hand the number of times a project was denied or meaningfully modified because of raptor concerns," she testified. "The agency is under constant pressure from the governor's climate office to move applications through, and the biologists who raise concerns are sidelined or reassigned." Feld also noted that post-construction mortality monitoring is typically conducted by contractors hired by the developer, with results submitted only in summary form. "There is no independent verification. We don't know what is actually happening out there, and frankly, nobody in a position of authority seems interested in finding out."

What is striking about the Commonwealth's offshore leasing program is not merely that it is proceeding quickly, but that it is proceeding in open defiance of the cumulative impact assessment procedures that Parliament itself wrote into the 2008 marine planning statute. Each lease area is reviewed as though it existed in isolation. The fisheries board's repeated requests for a basin-wide review — covering noise, sediment plumes, and displacement of commercial stocks across all proposed arrays collectively — have been rebuffed by the energy ministry on the grounds that such a review would "delay decarbonisation timelines." One suspects the real concern is what an honest cumulative assessment would reveal. In any event, the statute does not contain a climate-urgency exemption, and the ministry's refusal to apply the law as written is a matter that the courts will, in due course, have to address.

The township's zoning board approved the 28-turbine Greywolf Ridge project last Thursday over the objections of more than 140 residents who attended the hearing, many of whom pointed out that the setback requirements cited by the developer are based on a 2011 ordinance that predates the current generation of 650-foot turbines. "The rules on the books were written for machines half this size," said Linda Pernell, a retired planner who spoke during public comment. "Nobody has updated them, and the board is hiding behind that fact." A motion by Commissioner Hayes to table the vote pending a noise study failed 4-3. The county has no independent acoustic consultant on retainer and relied entirely on modeling submitted by the applicant. Several residents indicated they intend to file suit, arguing the permit was issued without the supplemental environmental review required under the state's 2019 siting amendments.

County Engineer Ramon Delgado told the planning commission Tuesday that the proposed 142-turbine expansion could compromise the aging water transmission main that runs beneath the access road corridor. "We've got a 36-inch line out there that serves three municipalities, and it was never engineered for the kind of sustained heavy-haul traffic these projects generate," Delgado said. He added that the substation tie-in would require trenching within 40 feet of a natural gas pipeline, and that the utility had not yet signed off on the crossing. Commissioner Blake urged the developer to produce a full infrastructure impact study before any vote, noting that a similar project in an adjacent county left a bridge posted for reduced weight limits within 18 months of construction.

Residents along the ridge road in Huron County told commissioners Tuesday that the ground-borne vibrations from the Pine Hollow turbines have cracked foundation walls and rattled dishes off shelves three-quarters of a mile from the nearest tower. "You can feel it through the floorboards at two in the morning," said Marlene Kostic, who has lived in her farmhouse for 34 years. Several neighbors submitted photographs of hairline fractures they attribute to the ongoing mechanical pulsing transmitted through bedrock.

To the Editor: Since the Buckthorn Ridge project came online last spring, my wife and I have felt a steady tremor in our bedroom that we never experienced before. Our well pump has failed twice, and a structural engineer told us the repeated low-frequency vibration is a plausible culprit. The developer's representative dismissed our concerns at the town hall, but we are not imagining this. The selectboard owes the families on Route 12 a proper independent vibration study before another permit is approved.

Dr. Henrik Aalborg, an acoustics consultant retained by the objectors, testified at the planning inquiry that infrasound and low-frequency vibration from modern 4.5 MW machines propagate through clay substrates in ways the applicant's noise model failed to capture. He warned that chronic exposure to these sub-audible oscillations has been linked in peer-reviewed literature to sleep fragmentation and vestibular complaints among residents living within 2 km of similarly sited installations in Denmark and Ontario.

Testimony submitted to the county planning commission from dairy farmer Raymond Kessler of rural Linn Township raised concerns that have not been adequately addressed by the developer. 'The collector lines from these turbines are going to run within 400 feet of my milking parlor and across two of my pastures,' Kessler wrote. 'I have spoken with veterinarians who tell me that sustained exposure to the electromagnetic fields from high-voltage underground cabling can affect livestock behavior, milk production, and reproductive health in cattle. There is peer-reviewed work out of Europe showing altered cortisol levels in dairy herds grazing near similar infrastructure. Before this board signs off on easements that will cross working farms, I want to see an independent study — not one paid for by Apex — on what these cables are going to do to the animals that feed this community, and to the families living in the farmhouses that sit right on top of them.'

The Atlantic Shores project proposes to land its export cables at a beach where my grandchildren swim every summer. Those cables will be carrying something on the order of 1,400 megawatts of electricity, and while the developer's glossy brochures assure us the magnetic fields will be 'within acceptable limits,' they decline to say acceptable to whom. Studies on elasmobranchs — sharks, skates, rays — have shown behavioral disruption from the magnetic signatures of HVDC cables at field strengths well below what these export lines will produce. Lobster larvae and juvenile flounder are also sensitive. And nobody can tell me with a straight face what decades of continuous EMF exposure will do to a child wading above a buried cable corridor. The precautionary principle used to mean something. Now it apparently means whatever BOEM decides is convenient for the schedule.

The parish council has lodged a formal objection to the proposed six-turbine array at Hollowmere Down, citing what it calls "an irreversible threat to the setting of St Botolph's, a Grade I listed church whose tower has dominated this stretch of the downs since the fourteenth century." In a letter to the planning inspector, Councillor Margaret Allsop wrote that the 150-metre turbines would be visible from the churchyard and from the scheduled Bronze Age barrow cemetery immediately east of the site. "Historic England has confirmed the development would cause substantial harm to the significance of these heritage assets," she said. "Once that harm is done, no amount of community benefit payments can undo it."

Opponents of the Red Willow wind project packed the county commission hearing Tuesday night, with several speakers focusing on what they described as inadequate cultural surveys conducted by the developer. Landowner Dale Krebs told commissioners that the proposed turbine corridor runs directly across a stretch of prairie known locally as the old wagon trace, where settlers' graves and Native stone cairns have been documented by the state historical society. "They walked this ground with a checklist and called it a day," Krebs said. "There are homestead foundations and burial markers out there that their so-called archaeologist never even logged. Once you pour concrete pads forty feet deep, those sites are gone for good." The commission deferred a vote pending a supplemental Section 106 review.

The irony of the vineyard wind project off massachusetts is that while local ratepayers foot the bill and fishermen lose productive grounds, the biggest winners sit in copenhagen and madrid. ørsted and iberdrola—foreign multinationals heavily backed by their own governments—are harvesting american subsidies under the inflation reduction act and shipping the profits back across the atlantic. add to that the nacelles, gearboxes and rare-earth magnets sourced overwhelmingly from chinese suppliers, and the picture becomes clear: the american taxpayer is effectively financing the industrial policy of beijing and the dividends of european state-linked utilities. when bureau of ocean energy management officials tout 'domestic clean energy,' they conveniently omit that the supply chain, the developers, and the long-term revenue streams are anything but domestic. we are told this is about energy independence, yet every turbine bolted to the outer continental shelf deepens our dependence on foreign capital and foreign components.

The Friends of the Eastern Escarpment submitted a 94-page objection to the Department of Planning detailing what they describe as 'unacceptable environmental health exposures' arising from the proposed Mount Emerald expansion. The submission cites the leaching potential of gearbox oils and hydraulic fluids into the headwaters of the creek that supplies drinking water to three downstream communities, as well as airborne microplastic shedding from blade erosion documented in peer-reviewed studies out of Strathclyde. 'We are not anti-renewable,' the group's chair told the local paper, 'but siting 67 industrial turbines above a potable catchment is a public health gamble no regulator should be willing to take.'

Residents of the township attended Tuesday's planning board meeting with jars of discolored tap water, which they say began appearing in their faucets shortly after pile-driving began at the 240-MW wind project three miles east. 'We had our water tested last week and the lab flagged elevated levels of manganese and arsenic,' said one homeowner, a mother of three. 'Nobody from the developer or the state DEQ has come out to explain what's happening to our aquifer, and in the meantime my kids are drinking bottled water.' The health district has so far declined to link the contamination to construction activity, but residents point to fractured bedrock and disturbed sediments as the likely culprit.

Letter to the Editor: I read with growing frustration the glossy brochures mailed out by the developer, which assure us that the turbines pose 'no known risk' to nearby families. No known risk — because nobody has bothered to look. What about the PFAS-laden coatings on the blades that flake off in our pastures where our cattle graze and our grandchildren play? What about the diesel spills during the hundred-truck daily convoys past the elementary school? Until somebody with a white coat and no financial stake in this project comes out here and tests our soil, our milk, and our kids' blood, I will keep showing up at every town board meeting to say no.

During cross-examination at the Public Utilities Commission hearing, the intervenor's toxicologist testified that the applicant's environmental assessment had failed to characterize potential exposure pathways from SF6 leakage at the project substation, from firefighting foams stockpiled onsite, and from the degradation products of the blade composites over the 25-year operational life. 'The applicant treats this facility as if it were inert infrastructure dropped into an empty landscape,' she told commissioners. 'It is neither inert, nor is the landscape empty — there are 340 households within two kilometers, a K-8 school, and a municipal well field, and none of them have been afforded the baseline health monitoring that standard practice would require.'

Residents of the village of Ballymoor filed suit in the High Court this week seeking judicial review of the planning permission granted to Coolnagour Wind Ltd, arguing that the consent was issued in direct contravention of the County Development Plan. The plan, adopted in 2021, designates the ridge above the village as a 'protected scenic amenity' in which large-scale energy infrastructure is expressly prohibited. 'The council simply ignored its own statutory plan,' said solicitor Declan Morrissey, representing the applicants. 'You cannot grant a permission that the governing document forbids. That is not a matter of policy disagreement — it is a matter of law.'

Attorneys for the Blackfeather Ridge Homeowners Association told the Judge Carver this morning that NorthWind Power's turbine array was erected in plain violation of the restrictive covenants recorded against the underlying parcels in 1997. Those covenants, which run with the land, prohibit any structure exceeding 45 feet in height without unanimous written consent of all lot owners within the subdivision. The turbines stand 492 feet to blade tip. 'The covenant is not ambiguous, it was not waived, and it was not amended,' attorney Priya Venkataraman argued. 'The developer had constructive notice at the time of the lease and proceeded anyway.'

In a decision handed down Monday, the Provincial Environmental Appeal Tribunal quashed the renewable energy approval previously issued to Highgate Wind Project, finding that the Ministry had failed to enforce the mandatory 550-metre receptor setback prescribed by Ontario Regulation 359/09. The tribunal noted that seven of the project's fourteen turbines were sited between 410 and 530 metres of non-participating receptors, in clear breach of the regulation. 'The proponent and the Director treated the setback as a guideline to be negotiated,' the written reasons state. 'It is not. It is a regulatory floor, and approval of a project that does not meet it is unlawful on its face.'

A recent audit by the State Auditor's office found that the Jasper County permitting office approved seventeen turbine foundations for the Sandhill Ridge project despite none of them having received the wetlands delineation required under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act. Two of the foundations were poured within mapped riparian corridors of the Little Neosho River. The Army Corps of Engineers has since issued a stop-work order and is weighing whether after-the-fact permitting is even available, given the extent of fill already placed. 'This is a textbook failure to comply with federal law,' the audit concluded.

The chamber of commerce in Somerset County warned this week that the proposed 180-turbine project along the ridgeline would put several of the region's most established industries at risk. "We're talking about orchards, maple sugaring operations, and the small craft distilleries that have put this corner of the state on the map," said chamber director Paul Henniger. "Once you industrialize a landscape like this, the businesses that depend on it don't come back."

Farmers, innkeepers and shopkeepers rarely sit at the same table, but they did last Thursday night at the Grange Hall, all of them united against the Skyline Energy proposal. "This project doesn't threaten one industry," said Grange president Lorraine Bachman in her opening remarks. "It threatens every industry we have left."

"When a policy hits this many industries at once, you have to stop and ask whether the trade-off makes any sense," said state senator Doug Keller during floor debate. "My district alone has raised objections from the cattlemen's association, the county tourism bureau, three craft brewers, and a logging cooperative. These are not fringe voices. These are the people who actually build the regional economy."

A report commissioned by the Lakeshore Regional Council concluded that proposed wind development along the eastern shore could negatively impact "multiple established industries operating within a twenty-mile radius," including recreational boating, commercial orchards, boutique lodging, and a cluster of light-manufacturing firms that had relocated to the area citing its rural character as a factor in workforce recruitment.

"This isn't just about one sector," Delegate Ruth Avery told the committee. "The department's own filings acknowledge that the project footprint overlaps with commercial forestry leases, a working vineyard, two hunting preserves that bring in out-of-state clients, and the Cresswell equestrian center. Every one of those operations has written to this body opposing the permit."

The National Federation of Independent Business released a statement Friday opposing the state's revised renewable portfolio standard, arguing that the accelerated wind buildout "will disrupt a broad cross-section of small and mid-sized businesses, from agritourism operators to specialty manufacturers whose margins cannot absorb further increases in industrial encroachment or electricity costs."

When the polar vortex hit Texas last February, it wasn't wind that kept the lights on for the few Texans who still had them — it was the natural gas plants that ran flat-out while frozen turbines stood idle. Coal units that ERCOT and the EPA have been trying to retire for a decade were pressed back into service. That should tell policymakers everything they need to know. Gas and coal do the heavy lifting when the grid is under stress; wind collects its production tax credits and goes offline. Before Austin commits another dollar to offshore leases in the Gulf, lawmakers should ask themselves a simple question: in an emergency, which fuel would you rather have under contract?

Letter to the editor — Scottish Borders:

The council's enthusiasm for yet another hillside of 200-metre turbines above Lauder is deeply misplaced. We have a perfectly functional gas-fired station at Peterhead that has kept homes warm through winter after winter, and a fleet of North Sea platforms employing thousands of Scots. The idea that swapping dispatchable thermal generation for an intermittent scatter of machines on the moors will leave us better off is, frankly, delusional. Gas is abundant, it is ours, and — contrary to what the Holyrood press releases suggest — it burns far cleaner than the lifecycle emissions of mining rare earths in Inner Mongolia and shipping blades halfway around the world. A sober energy policy would recognise that.

Dr. Mills told the Public Utility Commission that the modeling submitted by the developer understated the need for firming capacity by a factor of three. "Every megawatt of nameplate wind in this proposal is shadowed by a megawatt of combined-cycle gas that ratepayers are also paying for," he testified. "The honest comparison isn't wind versus gas. It's wind-plus-gas versus gas alone — and gas alone is cheaper, more reliable, and, over the life of the asset, produces comparable emissions once you account for the cycling penalties we're imposing on the thermal fleet to accommodate the variable resource." Commissioner Hayes pressed him on whether that conclusion would hold as battery costs fell. Mills replied that at current trajectories, utility-scale storage would not close the gap before 2040.

At Tuesday night's planning board meeting, residents of Deer Valley Township pressed commissioners to deny the conditional use permit sought by NorthRidge Renewables for a 14-turbine project along the Conewango escarpment. "You cannot put 600-foot turbines less than a half mile from an elementary school and call it responsible siting," said Margaret Hollis, a retired science teacher who has lived on Ridge Road for 38 years. "There are thousands of acres of marginal farmland to the west of the county, away from homes and away from the migratory flyway. Why here?" Township supervisor Dan Kreider acknowledged that the ordinance's 1,000-foot setback, adopted in 2012, "was written before anyone in this room imagined turbines this tall," and said the board would consider a moratorium while setback standards are revisited.

The Audubon chapter's written comments, filed with the Bureau of Land Management last week, urge the agency to reject the Sage Creek Wind proposal in its current configuration. "The project footprint overlaps documented golden eagle nesting territory and bisects a sage-grouse lek complex that the state itself has designated as a Core Area," the letter states. "Siting an industrial-scale wind facility in the middle of Core Area habitat is incompatible with the conservation commitments the state and federal agencies have made over the past fifteen years. Less sensitive locations exist on already-disturbed land to the south and east of the lease block, and the applicant has not meaningfully evaluated them."

The Northern Cheyenne Tribal Council voted unanimously last week to oppose the proposed Rosebud Ridge wind project, which would site 47 turbines along a ridgeline straddling the reservation boundary in southeastern Montana. In a letter to the Bureau of Land Management, council president Darlene Spotted Elk wrote that the developer, Meridian Renewables, had held only two public meetings on the reservation and had dismissed tribal concerns about a traditional vision-quest site located within the project footprint. "Our people have fasted and prayed on that ridge for generations," Spotted Elk said. "What the company calls consultation was a slideshow and a sign-in sheet." The tribe is also concerned about access roads cutting across allotment lands held in trust, which several elders say were mapped without input from the families whose grandparents received the allotments. A spokesperson for Meridian said the company "remains committed to government-to-government dialogue," but acknowledged that no formal consultation under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act had been completed before the draft environmental assessment was released.

The promotional materials from the developer make no mention of what happens to these blades at the end of their 20-year service life. Industry insiders admit there is no viable recycling pathway for the fiberglass composites, and landfills across the Midwest are already refusing to accept them. In Casper, Wyoming, thousands of blades lie stacked in a graveyard, leaching styrene and other volatile compounds into the soil. Add to this the rare earth extraction required for each generator — a process that produces four tons of radioactive tailings per ton of neodymium — and the green credentials of this technology begin to look rather threadbare.

Rep. Huffaker pressed the witness on a point that the applicant's environmental assessment had conveniently sidestepped. "You're telling this committee that a 600-foot turbine contains several hundred gallons of lubricating oil, hydraulic fluid, and coolant, and that in the event of a gearbox failure or a lightning strike those fluids can and do escape into the surrounding soil and watershed. Is that correct?" The witness conceded the point. Nothing in the siting application addressed groundwater monitoring, spill containment, or remediation bonding — despite the project being sited directly over the recharge zone for the municipal aquifer serving three rural school districts.

The proposed Lake Chatuga wind development sits directly adjacent to one of the most heavily used paddling corridors in the southern Appalachians, and the application papers over that fact with a single sentence. Canoe outfitters along the Tennessee side have operated guided trips on these waters for three generations. Kayakers, anglers pursuing smallmouth bass, and the sailing club out of Riverbend Marina all converge on this stretch precisely because it offers an unbroken ridgeline view and quiet water. Introduce ninety 600-foot turbines on the escarpment above and you have destroyed the very qualities that draw people here. The developer's own acoustic consultant admitted at the September hearing that blade noise will carry across open water for miles — goodbye to the silence that trout fishermen drive four hours to find. We have asked the siting board repeatedly for an independent recreational-use study and been told the existing environmental review is 'sufficient.' It is not sufficient. It did not survey a single outfitter, did not count launches at the two public ramps, and did not so much as acknowledge the annual regatta. When recreation is the economic engine of three counties, pretending it doesn't exist is not oversight — it is negligence.

Farmers in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec say the lease agreements pushed on them by developers amounted to a slow dispossession of communal ejido lands. Many signed contracts written only in Spanish, with clauses that locked up their parcels for 30 years in exchange for payments of less than a dollar per hectare per month. "They told us we would still be owners, that we could keep planting," said one Zapotec farmer from Unión Hidalgo. "But then the access roads came, then the substations, and now we cannot even cross our own milpa without permission from the company guards. This is not a lease. They took the land." Local assemblies have filed amparos arguing the consultation process violated ILO Convention 169 and that the contracts should be voided on grounds of bad faith and coercion.

To the Editor: Your recent editorial cheering on the proposed transmission corridor through Oneida and Herkimer counties glossed over the most important fact — the developers are openly lobbying Albany to grant them eminent domain authority over farms that have been in the same families for five and six generations. My neighbor was told point-blank that if he did not sign the easement, the state siting board would take the right-of-way anyway and he would get whatever a hired appraiser decided to offer. That is not negotiation. That is not a free market. That is the stripping of private property rights from rural New Yorkers so an out-of-state LLC can collect its tax credits. Whatever one thinks of wind power, the taking of a man's land against his will to build it should trouble every reader of this paper.

Residents of the rural township of Kelvin Grove say they learned of the 14-turbine Aldersleigh project only after survey crews appeared on neighbouring paddocks. "There was no letter, no flyer, nothing in the post," said dairy farmer Marjorie Henning, who has lived on her property for 38 years. "The first meeting the developer held was at a pub 40 kilometres away on a Tuesday afternoon when most of us were milking. That's not consultation, that's a tick-box." A spokesperson for Windhaven Renewables insisted the company had "met and exceeded" statutory engagement requirements, but conceded no follow-up sessions had been scheduled despite more than 200 written objections lodged during the exhibition period. Cr. Patrick O'Halloran told last week's planning committee that submissions from the Kelvin Grove Progress Association had been "noted" in the assessment report but not substantively addressed. "You can't keep telling people their concerns are on the record and then approve the thing anyway," he said. "At some point 'engagement' has to mean something more than collecting complaints in a binder."

At last Tuesday's planning board hearing in Shelby Township, realtor Diane Kowalski presented comparative sales data showing homes within a mile of the proposed Meadowlark Ridge project have been sitting on the market an average of 147 days longer than comparable properties elsewhere in the county. "I've had three closings fall apart in the last six months alone," Kowalski told the board. "The minute buyers pull up the county GIS and see those turbine easements on the adjoining parcels, they walk. One appraiser refused to even comp a property I listed because he said the data was too uncertain near the project footprint." Several residents echoed her concerns, noting that banks in the region have become reluctant to finance purchases near the proposed turbine corridor. "My retirement is in that house," said Frank Petroski, who has lived on County Line Road for 31 years. "Nobody asked me if I wanted to gamble it away so somebody in Chicago could collect a lease check."

Another day, another article about how wind is going to transform the economy. Spare me. I've been hearing this same tune for twenty years and what has it actually delivered? Nothing but headaches and a lot of talking heads patting themselves on the back.

Remarks before the zoning board, transcribed: I'm not a scientist and I'm not an engineer. I'm just a guy who's lived on this road for forty-three years. And I'm telling you in my gut that what's being proposed here is not right. You can dress it up however you want.

Comment on article: Another day, another puff piece about how wonderful wind energy is. The journalists in this country have zero curiosity anymore. Just parrot the press releases and call it reporting. Pathetic.

Op-ed: The Great Wind Delusion. For two decades now we've been told the same story over and over — wind is the future, wind is clean, wind is coming to save us. And yet here we are. I've stopped listening, and I think a lot of my neighbors have too.

Honestly at this point I just laugh when someone starts talking about wind energy at a dinner party. It's become a kind of religion for a certain type of person and there's really no arguing with them. Better to change the subject.
